gr26-027.title: Roaming over the Horseback
gr26-027.syn: Against a landscape of grasslands and mines, a man searches for identity and meaning between tradition and personal values.
gr26-027.bio: Bai Runqing directed and co-wrote A Qintu's Autumn (with Liu Jiarui), his first feature, registered by Beijing Songta Pictures with Sun Tao producing and Xia Gang supervising. The project reached the top 8 of the final pitch in the work-in-progress section of the 6th Golden Rooster Film Pitch in 2024.
highlights: An injured Mongolian rider returns to the steppe and remounts amid loss and farewell.
Bai Runqing's first feature, supervised by Xia Gang.
Steppe urbanisation and young people's unease are central.
Reached the top 8 of the final pitch at the 2024 Golden Rooster Film Pitch.
gr26-027.st:
The registered synopsis: a racehorse jockey returns home to recover from injury, faces a friend leaving and uncertainty about his future, and finally follows his heart and rides again, reunited with a dream he had lost. At the Golden Rooster post-screening talk the director said the film wants to capture the quiet losses in life, comings and goings of family and friends, often realised only afterward; Sechin is making a solemn farewell to constant loss, and he hoped to bring warmth into that mood of parting.

He puts into the story his observation of urbanisation on the grassland and the unease of young people moving between town and country: the steppe takes in Sechin's injury and regrets and also accepts those who choose to leave. In public materials, his horse possibly being taken to settle a debt and old friends leaving are the real pressures he faces. Posters and stills often use long lenses to place the figures in the vast grassland. Starring Bayin, Tumenbayar and Taozi.

It screened at the Golden Rooster domestic film showcase in November 2026 and is reported to be expected in cinemas in 2027.

gr26-028.title: Daughter of the River
gr26-028.syn: Writer Hong Ying revisits her childhood in Chongqing, confronting hunger, family secrets and her difficult bond with her mother.
gr26-028.bio: Hong Ying, born in Chongqing in 1962, is a British-Chinese novelist, poet and director whose autobiographical novel Daughter of the River has been translated into more than 30 languages. Her first film as director was Moonlight Warrior in 2021, and Daughter of the River is her second, adapting the novel in documentary form.
highlights: Adapted from Hong Ying's autobiographical novel, three generations of women from 1940 to 2024.
Black-and-white alternates with colour; three actors play Hong Ying in turn.
Hong Ying appears with her real daughter Serpa.
Scheduled for national release on 8 March 2027.
gr26-028.st:
Adapted from Daughter of the River, the 101-minute film spans 1940 to 2024 and tells of three generations of women, grandmother, mother and daughter, across more than eighty years; black-and-white and colour alternate, the black-and-white carrying history and the colour looking back at the present. Hong Ying appears as narrator, with Wang Xiaoxi, Jiang Yujie and Hong Ying herself successively playing her childhood, youth and adulthood; her real interactions with daughter Serpa are also in the film. The line 'grandmother swims in the water, mother runs on the ground, so the daughter can fly in the sky' sums up its theme.

Critics call it a 'third kind', neither an ordinary documentary nor fiction: people and events come from real life, performed by actors. Hong Ying spent three years making it by hand: only seven people including driver and make-up artist when it started, investors turning away on hearing it was a documentary, so she paid with her royalties and borrowed money, even carrying the camera herself. Because the childhood No. 6 courtyard and its street have vanished, she wanted to commemorate those who left no names in the hungry years.

It previewed in Beijing on 24 October 2026 and is scheduled for national release on 8 March 2027.

gr26-029.title: Good Trip
gr26-029.syn: A family trip brings a father and his grown children into renewed contact, exposing old wounds and unspoken feelings.
gr26-029.bio: Heiward Mak and Wong Kam co-directed Good Trip, with Mak also writing; their earlier films include Golden Gate (2019) and The Lyricist Wannabe (2023), both close to personal experience. Supervised by Mabel Cheung, it received HK$9 million from the Hong Kong Film Development Fund's Fire Next Generation scheme, two to three times the budgets of their earlier work.
highlights: Nick Cheung and Chung Suet-ying as father and daughter on a road trip from the New Territories via Macau to Okinawa.
HK$9 million from the Fire Next Generation scheme, supervised by Mabel Cheung.
Draws on The Separated Soul so that someone whose body cannot travel journeys by imagination, refusing a plain tearjerker.
About 284 effects shots; grossed about HK$13 million in three weeks.
gr26-029.st:
Mok Chun-keung (Nick Cheung) is hospitalised with a serious illness while his daughter Chi-shan (Chung Suet-ying), a film art-department assistant, shuttles between set and hospital. On a last-minute errand to fetch a big soup bowl from the prop store, her father insists on coming along, and the two slip out of the hospital overnight on a trip from the New Territories to Macau and on to Okinawa, making up for his regrets.

The directors agreed not to adapt their own lives directly but to gather material from people around them: a father who loves pun jokes and speaks bluntly, Mak's own father who had unknowingly worked as an extra, and her last trip to Okinawa with him all found their way in. Extending the Tang tale The Separated Soul, she lets someone whose body cannot travel journey by imagination, hence the multiple universes and mixed modern and period costume; the directors say they did not want to make death a mere tearjerker. Reportedly there are about 284 effects shots, with many close-ups of the Okinawa rope-pulling scene shot against green screen.

It opened in Hong Kong on 15 October 2026 and grossed about HK$13 million in three weeks.

gr26-030.title: Someone Like Me
gr26-030.syn: An intimate relationship challenges prejudice about disability, bodily autonomy, desire and the right to love.
gr26-030.bio: Tam Wai-ching is a Hong Kong director and writer whose earlier feature was the opening film of the 14th Hong Kong Asian Film Festival. Someone Like Me is her second feature, supervised by Stanley Kwan and Kwan Tung-chiu, with Patrick Cheung Shu-ping as editing consultant.
highlights: Fish Liew won Best Actress at the 44th Hong Kong Film Awards for the role.
Starts from disabled people's intimacy and bodily autonomy; supervised by Stanley Kwan and Kwan Tung-chiu.
World premiere in the Women's Empowerment section of the Tokyo International Film Festival.
Rated Category III (18+) in Hong Kong.
gr26-030.st:
Born with cerebral palsy, the upbeat Ah Mui (Fish Liew) earns a living by painting and has friends who also use wheelchairs and skateboard. Her over-protective mother insists on arranging a hysterectomy, shaking Ah Mui's sense of control over her own body. Encouraged by her friend Joe, she learns of a self-organised volunteer group providing sexual services for disabled people and meets a volunteer, Ken. Starting from the relationship of volunteer and client, feelings grow between them as they face moral doubts, physical limits and social acceptance.

The film was shot in January 2024, had its world premiere in the Women's Empowerment section of the Tokyo International Film Festival on 31 October 2025, opened in Hong Kong on 27 November with a Category III rating (18+), and returned to Emperor cinemas in April 2026.

At the 44th Hong Kong Film Awards in 2026, Fish Liew won Best Actress and her co-lead was nominated for Best Actor.

gr26-031.title: Atlantic Rhapsody
gr26-031.syn: After accidentally cooking a supermarket's ornamental shark, a worker follows mysterious sounds and an old missing-person notice back to his hometown.
gr26-031.bio: Zhong Kaifeng, born after 1995, made Atlantic Rhapsody as his first feature, co-written with Wu Linfeng. He earlier made a four-minute short, Swimming in a Whale, and the film grew out of an experimental music band he formed with friends and a news item from 2005.
highlights: Best Film in the main competition of the 2026 Shanghai Golden Goblet Awards.
A 'sound-watching' film with sound as its core, born of experimental music.
A cooked ornamental shark, auditory hallucinations and a search for a father in the northeast.
Starring Yin Fang, Wang Yitong, Li Xueqin and Huang Miyi.
gr26-031.st:
Supermarket shelf-stacker Ding Mao (Wang Yitong) accidentally cooks the store's ornamental shark and starts hearing a strange sound. A steel nail found in a sausage leads to a missing-person notice that has lain dormant for ten years, and he returns from a southern city to his long-left hometown in the northeast to look for his father. Through an abandoned amusement park, a winter zoo, a supermarket selling shark meat, an experimental musician, a blind fortune-teller who understands animals, a trainer whose legs were bitten off by a shark and a mysterious picture-book painter, he pieces together the absurd fragments of his father Ding Jianguo's life (Yin Fang).

Called a 'sound-watching' film, it uses sound as its central narrative carrier. The title comes from the old TV series The Man from Atlantis, which recurs in the film; his father, a strong swimmer, is nicknamed 'Ding Mike'. The director notes that many sharks must keep swimming to stay alive, much like his father's way of surviving. The script was first called Swimming in a Whale and was revised over several years of pitching; it reached the top ten of the Chinese Directors Guild's Green Onion programme and was a winning project of the 2022 Golden Rooster 'Light of Art' pitch.

It had its world premiere at the 28th Shanghai International Film Festival on 18 June 2026 in the Golden Goblet main competition and won Best Film.

gr26-032.title: Deep Quiet Room
gr26-032.syn: A husband's anticipation of parenthood gives way to grief after his wife's death, revealing painful secrets in her family.
gr26-032.bio: Shen Ko-shang is a Taiwanese director long known for documentaries; Deep Quiet Room is his first narrative feature, adapted from Lin Hsiu-ho's novel of the same name and co-written with Lu Hsin-chih. Before 2019 he did extensive research on domestic violence and concluded that filming real people for a documentary raised serious ethical problems, so he turned to the fictional buffer of a drama.
highlights: Fei Mu Honour for Best Film, Best Actor and Audience Award at the 9th Pingyao festival.
Seven nominations at the 62nd Golden Horse Awards.
The first narrative feature by documentary director Shen Ko-shang, adapted from Lin Hsiu-ho's novel.
Starring Joseph Chang, Ariel Lin and King Shih-chieh.
gr26-032.st:
Yu-ming (Joseph Chang) and Yi-ting (Ariel Lin) meet and fall in love in the 'deep quiet room' of a university library. After she becomes pregnant, Yi-ting's emotions unravel and she asks for an abortion and a divorce; her disabled father (King Shih-chieh) moves in. Yu-ming cannot read her mind until he finds a manuscript she was editing and realises how much more she had borne. The film moves on two timelines, using handheld camera, tilted shots and sound design to convey suppression and power, with silence as its core image.

A Taiwan–Italy co-production running 107 minutes, it premiered at the 9th Pingyao International Film Festival on 28 September 2025, winning the Fei Mu Honour for Best Film, Best Actor and the Audience Award, and received seven nominations at the 62nd Golden Horse Awards. It opened in Taiwan on 20 March 2026, rated for viewers aged 16 and over.

It deals with domestic violence and childhood trauma in a restrained manner; the director has said he wanted to address crises in ordinary families rather than simply suffering.

gr26-033.title: The Waves Will Carry Us
gr26-033.syn: Returning to Malaysia for his father's funeral, a man encounters a dispute over the body and a family's tangled religious identities.
gr26-033.bio: Lau Kek Huat was born in Malaysia and works mainly in Taiwan, with credits including the feature Boluomi, and the documentaries Absent without Leave and From Island to Island. Boluomi and Absent without Leave were banned in Malaysia for touching on the history of the Malayan Communist Party; The Waves Will Carry Us is his first narrative feature released in Malaysian cinemas.
highlights: Five nominations at the 62nd Golden Horse Awards, with Vera Chen winning Best Supporting Actress.
Based on a real Malaysian 'body snatching' case, handled with black humour.
Lau Kek Huat's first narrative feature released in Malaysia.
Shot in both Malaysia and Taiwan.
gr26-033.st:
Ah Yao (Wei Chun-chan), who has long worked in Taiwan, returns to Malaysia to bury his father with his siblings, only to meet the religious department claiming that the father had secretly converted to Islam and must be buried in a Muslim cemetery. The three siblings react differently: the eldest yields, brother Ah Choy (Lu Yang) confronts, and sister Shui-yun (Vera Chen) strives to keep the ritual intact. As the funeral proceeds it also brings out a smuggler's past, Southeast Asian durians, fever and an identity card never obtained. The story draws on a real 'body snatching' case and is handled with black humour.

The title comes from the Hokkien phrase for life's ups and downs and is also tied to Chen Lei's song Be Happy; the English title means that waves carry people forward. The director has said that his first child was born while he wrote, and he typed with one hand while holding the baby, asking himself whether this could be filmed. Shot in Malaysia and Taiwan, it was supported by Taiwan's Ministry of Culture film bureau and TAICCA among others.

It premiered on 18 October 2025 at the Hawaii International Film Festival, received five nominations at the 62nd Golden Horse Awards with Vera Chen winning Best Supporting Actress, and opened in Malaysia in April 2026 after the censors made six cuts.

gr26-034.title: Life of Jorge Luis Borges
gr26-034.syn: Archival materials, poetry, travel and playful narration turn a biography of Jorge Luis Borges into a labyrinthine cinematic investigation.
gr26-034.bio: Mariano Llinás is an Argentine director often described as among the most Borgesian of contemporary filmmakers, drawn to nested structures and endlessly branching narratives. His previous film La Flor consists of six distinct episodes shot over a decade around the world with about a hundred participants and runs 808 minutes. He works with producer Laura Citarella at El Pampero Cine, whose latest production is Life of Jorge Luis Borges.
highlights: World premiere at Venice; 323 minutes in three parts.
Llinás and Borges expert Montequín track down manuscripts and clues.
From Geneva and New York to Iceland, narrated on the move.
Llinás appears on screen as narrator and keeps interrupting himself.
gr26-034.st:
The film had its world premiere out of competition at Venice in 2026, then played Toronto's Wavelengths, the New York Film Festival and the London Film Festival. It runs 323 minutes in three parts. Llinás teams up with Borges expert Ernesto Montequín, and, like Holmes and Watson, they search manuscripts, letters, postcards, diaries and photographs, following places Borges lived in, passed through or alluded to, from Geneva and Brooklyn to Iceland.

In a Film Comment interview Llinás said that Borges had written and unwritten his own biography at the same time, so the question was how to deal with those tricks from another angle. He interrupts himself constantly and argues that life enters writing through digressions. The film is a biography and also lets us watch how such a film is made.

Reviewers variously call it a mix of travelogue, reenactment, investigative journalism and essay, or one of the most enjoyable literary films in years; others note that for a five-hour-plus biography it does not aim to be comprehensive.

gr26-035.title: Admission
gr26-035.syn: Parents and their advisers investigate what went wrong when a six-year-old is placed on a prestigious school's rejection list.
gr26-035.bio: Quentin Hsu worked with Beijing Film Academy students on several projects while at university, and his directing debut was the 2008 short Catching Cold. He assisted a number of Chinese directors for several years; his screenplay (Sex) Appeal (2014) premiered at the Busan International Film Festival and was nominated for an Asian New Talent Award at the Shanghai International Film Festival. Over the past decade he has written and produced film and series projects with Coolie Films. Admission is his first feature, and he says he is interested in people's tendency toward self-deception and its causes.
highlights: Quentin Hsu's first feature, premiered at Tallinn Black Nights in the First Feature Competition.
A hunt for who is to blame for a school rejection, set in one hotel room with a chamber-play structure.
A board member, an admissions agent and the couple turn on each other, peeling away their polite surfaces.
Uses a school interview to explore parents' anxiety about a child's future and their own worth.
gr26-035.st:
A couple tries to get their six-year-old son into an elite international school. After the interview, word spreads that he has been rejected, so they meet two trusted helpers, a board member and an admissions agent, in a hotel room to find out who is to blame.

The story is kept almost entirely within one enclosed space. As suspicion deepens, each person's hidden motives and quiet frustrations come out. School admission becomes a way to talk about parents' anxieties over success, security and self-worth. The Tallinn Black Nights programme files it under satire and parent-child relationships, and describes it as a chamber piece that distils the pressure of modern parenthood.

gr26-036.title: The Violinist
gr26-036.syn: War separates two aspiring violinists in 1941; a treasured instrument reconnects later generations with their story.
gr26-036.bio: Ervin Han is a Singaporean director and writer and sits on the industry advisory committee of NTU's School of Art, Design and Media; he spent more than a decade pushing The Violinist forward, calling it a deeply personal creative mission. Co-director Raúl García is a Spanish animator whose credits include Disney's Aladdin and Fantasia 2000, and he oversaw animation direction and visual storytelling.
highlights: Annecy Cristal for a Feature Film and SACEM award for Best Original Soundtrack; the first Singaporean feature in Annecy's competition.
Hand-drawn animation spanning 1941 to the present.
An old violin leads to two violinists torn apart by war.
A Singapore-Spain-Italy co-production.
gr26-036.st:
The film is a hand-drawn Singapore-Spain-Italy co-production by Robot Playground Media, TV ON Producciones and Altri Occhi, co-written by Han and Jordan Katherine See. Deadline describes a Spanish reporter investigating the origins of an old violin and uncovering the intertwined lives of two lovers, beginning in 1941 when the Japanese invasion of Malaya shatters the dreams of two young violinists, Kai and Fei, and extending to the present day.

In June 2026 it won the Cristal for a Feature Film and the SACEM Award for Best Original Soundtrack at the 50th Annecy festival; it was the first Singaporean feature in Annecy's official competition and Singapore's first animated feature in about 15 years. It opened in Singapore on 17 September and opens in Spain on 13 November; at the 2026 National Day Rally, Prime Minister Lawrence Wong praised Han's decade-long perseverance.

gr26-037.title: Bird of Paradise
gr26-037.syn: A middle-aged homemaker secretly takes pole-dancing lessons and begins to imagine a life beyond her family's expectations.
gr26-037.bio: Joey Wu is a new-generation Hong Kong director, and Bird of Paradise is her first feature, which she wrote and directed. The script won support under the seventh College Group of Hong Kong's First Feature Film Initiative, which allowed it to be made. She says the story grew from wanting to encourage her own mother, and everyone, to value themselves.
highlights: Joey Wu's first feature, a winner in the College Group of the 7th First Feature Film Initiative.
The heroine carries the real name of the director's mother, and daily details come from her.
Starring Catherine Chau, Elaine Jin, Peter Chan, Yeung Nga Man and Jayden Cheung.
Uses pole dancing as the way into a housewife's dream and freedom.
gr26-037.st:
The film grew out of the director's own mother. Wu named the heroine Yeung Mei-yuen after her mother's real name, and details such as making vegetable juice, cooking goji pasta, haggling over pork and the veins showing on an arm carrying heavy groceries come from her mother's daily care for the family. She says this is another way of appreciating what her mother gives.

In the story, Mei-yuen has spent years revolving around her husband and son in a monotonous routine. She chances upon pole dancing and, with the support of her mother Fung-mui, secretly learns it behind the back of her conservative husband and rebellious son, making friends along the way, including a classmate her son has a crush on. When the secret comes out, a family crisis follows. Catherine Chau learned pole dancing from scratch for the role and was reportedly injured during training before shooting began.

gr26-038.title: A Man of His Time
gr26-038.syn: In 1940 Vichy, an impoverished inventor's desire for recognition draws him into the machinery of an oppressive regime.
gr26-038.bio: Emmanuel Marre is a French director. In 2021 he co-directed Zero Fucks Given with Julie Lecoustre, which played in Cannes Critics' Week and won the Gan Foundation Award; his 2018 short Castle to Castle took two prizes at Locarno. Notre Salut (A Man of His Time) is his second feature, the first he has directed on his own; it competed at Cannes and won Best Screenplay. It draws on his great-grandfather Henri Marre, a committed Pétainist; Marre has said he wanted to capture the faces behind the major historical figures, the people in the background.
highlights: Best Screenplay at Cannes, plus the Prix des Cinémas Art et Essai, a special mention for the Citizenship Prize, and the Gillo Pontecorvo Award in Rome.
Based on letters between the director's great-grandparents: an 'ordinary man' who offers his services to the Vichy regime.
The French title is Henri's self-published manifesto 'Our Salvation'; the film asks not about a monster but about how a man with real feelings and ambition becomes part of the machine.
Swann Arlaud stars; crash zooms, blocking and anachronistic electronic music make history both satirical and disquieting.
gr26-038.st:
The film had its world premiere on 20 May 2026 in the Cannes competition. Marre drew on letters between his great-grandfather Henri Marre and his great-grandmother. In September 1940, 49-year-old Henri arrives alone in Vichy with his self-published manifesto Notre Salut ('Our Salvation', which gives the film its French title), offering his technical talents and ideals to the new regime. His abilities and lack of moral qualms are quickly noticed, and the film follows him as he becomes one cog in a machinery of oppression.

It won Best Screenplay at Cannes, the Prix des Cinémas Art et Essai and a special mention for the Citizenship Prize, then the Gillo Pontecorvo Award at the Rome Film Festival, and played in the Horizons section at Karlovy Vary. Marre said he deliberately gave Henri sincere feelings for his wife, since that is more powerful in questioning the figure of the monster. Screen Daily praised Swann Arlaud's performance but found the film overlong; Roger Ebert compared it to The Death of Stalin, saying that crash zooms and blocking make Henri look small in every scene, and noted the deliberately anachronistic house music.
gr26-038.editorial: Worth seeing if Vichy France and the banality of evil interest you. It is long and cool in tempo; don't expect plot thrills. Watch how the camera makes Henri look small, and the increasingly cold letters between him and his wife.
gr26-038.contentNote: Available story information indicates: Nazi-era persecution and its aftermath; Discrimination or abuse of power. Detailed depiction and intensity have not been verified; consider your individual needs.

gr26-039.title: Tai Chi Master
gr26-039.syn: Two childhood friends take opposing paths toward power, while one discovers a new martial art through adversity and nature.
gr26-039.bio: Yuen Woo-ping comes from a martial arts family; his father Yuen Siu-tien played Beggar So in Drunken Master. He made his name directing Snake in the Eagle's Shadow and Drunken Master, and later choreographed The Matrix and Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon, bringing Hong Kong kung fu's wirework and action design to the world. Tai Chi Master was produced by and stars Jet Li.
highlights: The first pairing of Jet Li and Michelle Yeoh, with Li also producing.
Loosely based on the origin legend of tai chi: a feud of Shaolin brothers over power.
Directed by Yuen Woo-ping, in the wirework and tight-cut action style of the 1990s.
Spun off in 1996 as Tai Chi Boxer.
gr26-039.st:
Released in Hong Kong on 18 November 1993 and made by Eastern Production, with Golden Harvest distributing, the film was written by Kwong Kim Yip, shot by Tom Lau and scored by Wu Wai-lap, with Jet Li also producing. Based loosely on the legend of the origin of tai chi, it has Jet Li as Zhang Junbao and Chin Siu-ho as Dong Tianbao, two boys at Shaolin who become enemies over different choices about power and life; Michelle Yeoh plays the female lead.

It was the first pairing of Jet Li and Michelle Yeoh, who later worked together in Hollywood on The Mummy: Tomb of the Dragon Emperor. Yuen Woo-ping directed and handled the martial arts choreography.

The film led to a 1996 spin-off, Tai Chi Boxer.
honors: 入选｜2026 Golden Rooster Film Screening · 功夫·功夫：华语经典展映
gr26-039.editorial: A good sample of 1990s Hong Kong wirework and tai chi action design; the plot is a traditional tale of chivalry and friendship, to be enjoyed relaxed.

gr26-040.title: Wakesurf Lovers
gr26-040.syn: An online critic unexpectedly becomes a surfing coach's student, and their growing relationship challenges his assumptions.
gr26-040.bio: Andrew Fung is a Hong Kong screenwriter and director who made his name with the TVB series Greed of Man. In film he has worked with leading figures, including Johnnie To on Sparrow and Changing Times during the Milkyway Image period, and wrote on several Stephen Chow films such as Shaolin Soccer, CJ7, Journey to the West: Conquering the Demons and The Mermaid. Wakesurf Lovers is based on his original story, with Fung as writer and director and Weng Ziguang as producer.
highlights: Billed as the first Chinese-language film about wakesurfing, shot on location in Hong Kong waters.
Starring Jeffrey Ngai and Renci Yeung, produced by Weng Ziguang.
Uses a storm started by online mockery to talk about piling-on criticism and learning to trust again.
Director Andrew Fung brings years of screenwriting on films by Stephen Chow and Johnnie To.
gr26-040.st:
Set around wakesurfing, the film is presented as the first Chinese-language film on the sport, mixing light comedy, coming of age and online public shaming. Surf instructor Sun Man is falsely accused and shamed online, and Chuan, a novice who knows nothing about surfing, posts a satirical clip under an online handle that unexpectedly goes viral. When he finds that the person he mocked was smeared, he signs up for her lessons under his real name and gradually turns from a keyboard troll into the person working hardest to clear her name.

The film was shot entirely on location in Hong Kong waters. The crew arrived at dawn each day with camera boats, rescue boats and an aerial platform to wait for good conditions, and the director says one surfing shot took more than 30 takes over two hours. Visual effects were mainly used to remove background boats and safety lines. Jeffrey Ngai and Renci Yeung trained intensively for several months before shooting.
honors: 入选｜2026 Golden Rooster Film Screening · 拾光：华语新片展映
gr26-040.editorial: A summery light comedy that uses surfing to ask how to face mistakes after misunderstanding and public shaming. Good for viewers who want something relaxed with a real-world theme, and the on-water footage suits the big screen.
gr26-040.contentNote: Available story information indicates: Exclusion or prejudice; Dangerous situations or accidents. Detailed depiction and intensity have not been verified; consider your individual needs.

gr26-041.title: Afterpiece
gr26-041.syn: A theatre director's new production entangles actors, marriage and past relationships as performance and private life blur.
gr26-041.bio: Keane Wong Tak-Kin is a Hong Kong director. Afterpiece is the feature he directed, and it received Golden Horse nominations for Best Leading Actress and Best Original Screenplay at the 63rd Golden Horse Awards.
highlights: Follows a stage director in creative paralysis, with life and play seeping into each other.
Nominated at the 63rd Golden Horse Awards for Best Leading Actress and Best Original Screenplay.
A former lover, a failing marriage and a young newcomer cross as three relationship threads.
Cantonese dialogue, 112 minutes.
gr26-041.st:
The film's protagonist Owen was once a celebrated stage director and has been trapped in creative paralysis for a decade. His former lover returns, and his wife drifts toward betrayal. In a desperate gamble to reclaim his dignity, he decides to write, direct and star in a new play.

During auditions he becomes dangerously drawn to Hanna, an untrained newcomer. As rehearsals begin, the line between the theatre and his crumbling reality becomes ever harder to see. The film is in Cantonese, and a Malaysian cinema chain lists it as a drama for adult audiences.

gr26-042.title: Dead Tide
gr26-042.syn: A former prisoner returns to a fishing village seeking forgiveness and encounters a woman being held captive.
gr26-042.bio: Kethsvin Chee is a Malaysian director. Dead Tide is his second feature, after Hello! Tapir (2020), which was nominated for Best Visual Effects at the Golden Horse Awards. The film is produced by Jin Ong and Sinje Lee, who worked on Abang Adik, with Angelica Lee as executive producer and co-writer.
highlights: Based on real people from the director's home fishing village.
Starring Chen Zeyao and Li Mu, with Angelica Lee and Wang Lilin producing.
The project was shortlisted at the Hong Kong-Asia Film Financing Forum in the In-Development category.
Selected for the Pingyao Crouching Tiger competition and nominated for five Golden Horse awards.
gr26-042.st:
The story is based on real people from Chee's hometown, a fishing village in Kuala Selangor, and was inspired by a cousin and a neighbour. When his mother told him that the woman had died, he kept thinking of her smiling face even though the world had not treated her well, and he wanted to capture that smile in a film.

Ten years ago Zhong was jailed for accidentally killing a young man from a neighbouring village. After his father's death he returns home hoping to find the victim's family and ask for forgiveness, but they have moved away. He meets Xue, a woman confined to a stilt house by her family, and the two forgotten people slowly grow close under the tide and moonlight. The director explains that the Chinese title refers to the Kuroshio, a warm current in the sea that stands for the love the characters find in a harsh reality, while the English title Dead Tide hints at calm, brief and precious moments.

gr26-043.title: Strangers in the Mountain
gr26-043.syn: Two police officers revisit a woman's disappearance in a remote village, uncovering emotional ties and conflicting versions of the past.
gr26-043.bio: Wan Bo is a Chinese director who also works in cinematography, and Strangers in the Mountain is his second feature. His first feature Chao was selected for the Chinese Cinema New Wave section of the 26th Shanghai International Film Festival, the 16th Macao International Film Festival and the 30th Kolkata International Film Festival. For this film he worked with Luo Pan, who wrote the script and shot the film, and Li Yixiao stars and also produces.
highlights: Wan Bo's second feature, with its world premiere in the Asian New Talent section of the 2026 Shanghai festival.
Black-and-white images that combine Jiangnan landscapes with an Eastern sensibility.
Luo Pan wrote and shot it, and Li Yixiao stars and produces.
The project won a special jury recommendation at the Shanghai festival's project market in 2024.
gr26-043.st:
The film is set in the mountains by Shan Creek in Zhejiang in the 1990s. Two police officers come to the mountains to look for a suspect in a woman's disappearance that has gone unsolved for seven years. As the questioning proceeds, the people connected to the case are drawn back into memories of the missing woman, Zhang Xue. A Deep Focus piece notes that the film avoids the usual detective-puzzle route and puts its weight on the characters' inner psychological maze.

The project's path is closely tied to the Shanghai International Film Festival. In 2024 it was selected for the festival's project market and received a special recommendation from the jury, and it began shooting in Hangzhou in late November that year. It returned in 2025 as a work in progress, and in 2026 it had its world premiere in the Asian New Talent section of the 28th festival. It is shot in black and white and combines Jiangnan landscapes, local dialect and an ensemble narrative.

gr26-044.title: When Malan Blooms
gr26-044.syn: Children from the mountains of Fuping overcome practical and musical challenges to sing at the Beijing Winter Olympics.
gr26-044.bio: Ma Xiaojing teaches at the Beijing Film Academy and was head of performance management for the opening and closing ceremonies of the Beijing Winter Olympics. At the end of 2021 she went to the mountains of Fuping in Hebei with the task of selecting a group to sing the Olympic anthem, based on director Zhang Yimou's idea of the fragrance of the earth. There she met the children of the Malan Flower Children's Choir and Deng Xiaolan, who had volunteered as a teacher in Malan village for 18 years. Ma wrote and directed When Malan Blooms and is its chief producer, and the teacher An Ran in the film is based on herself.
highlights: Based on the real story of the Fuping Malan Flower Children's Choir reaching the Winter Olympics stage.
Director Ma Xiaojing was the ceremonies' performance manager and is one of the story's models.
Starring Ni Dahong and Huang Mengying, with the choir's teachers and children playing themselves.
Received a jury nomination for Best Children's Film at the 39th Golden Rooster Awards.
gr26-044.st:
The film draws on real events. At the end of 2021 the Winter Olympics ceremonies team came to Fuping to select a group to sing the Olympic anthem. Led by teacher Deng Xiaolan and the head of the village school, the mountain children overcame many difficulties and finally sang the Olympic Hymn in Greek on the stage of the Games' opening and closing ceremonies. Ma says the film began for two reasons: Deng Xiaolan hoped before her death that Ma would make a film about the choir, and the children made a ten-year promise with her at the Bird's Nest.

The film was shot entirely on location in Fuping, with Ni Dahong and Huang Mengying joined by the teachers and children of the choir playing themselves. Its start of shooting was announced at the National Stadium in March 2025, and it later appeared at the 16th Beijing International Film Festival.

gr26-045.title: Nowhere to Lay My Eyes
gr26-045.syn: An experimental filmmaker visits her mother on Jeju Island and reconsiders family responsibility, ageing and artistic life.
gr26-045.bio: Hong Sangsoo was born in Seoul in 1960 and is one of the most prolific Korean directors: Nowhere to Lay My Eyes is his 35th feature, and The Day She Returns premiered at the Berlinale earlier the same year. He won the Golden Leopard at Locarno in 2015 for Right Now, Wrong Then and has won several Silver Bears in Berlin; he writes and directs, and often shoots, edits and scores his films himself. He has worked for years with Kim Min-hee, and this film marks her return to the screen after a maternity break.
highlights: Best Director at Locarno; Hong's 35th feature, in a year when The Day She Returns also premiered in Berlin.
Two days on Jeju, with meals, drink and talk; distance and care within a family hide in ordinary conversation.
Kim Min-hee returns after a maternity break as narrator and lead; Variety calls her performance restrained but more than meets the eye.
A crisp, bright image, a rare use of narration, and a closing short of the heroine's own: a dandelion growing in weeds.
gr26-045.st:
The film had its world premiere on 13 August 2026 in the main competition at the 79th Locarno Film Festival, then played in the main slate of the New York Film Festival alongside The Day She Returns; Cinema Guild has North American rights, and Hong won Best Director at Locarno. It runs just 72 minutes.

The story follows Sanghee (Kim Min-hee), a maker of experimental shorts, who travels with her brother to Jeju Island to visit their mother and meets her new husband, played by Kwon Hae-hyo, who is also a filmmaker. Most of the film unfolds over two days around meals, drinking and talk, from European furniture to documentary filmmaking, touching on intergenerational disappointment and misunderstanding. Variety called it as classically and welcomingly Hong as it gets, with Kim's restrained, more-than-meets-the-eye performance filling the blanks in his lean script.

Unlike some of his recent experiments in which story and imagery are left out of focus, the image here is crisp and bright, and there is a rare use of narration, spoken by Kim. It ends on one of Sanghee's own shorts, a dandelion growing in weeds. Roger Ebert's review reads it as a meditation on art, death and impermanence, which also sets love against solitude and documentary against fiction.
gr26-045.editorial: A fine entry point even if you haven't seen Hong before: short, and clear in story. Notice how seemingly offhand table talk gradually reveals the characters' disappointments, and how Sanghee's own short echoes the ending.
gr26-045.contentNote: Available story information indicates: Ageing and care; Family conflict or separation. Detailed depiction and intensity have not been verified; consider your individual needs.

gr26-046.title: We Are Born Good
gr26-046.syn: A mistaken restaurant order escalates into mutual revenge, exposing two city dwellers' desperation and unexpected need for support.
gr26-046.bio: Yeung Leung Chuen is a Hong Kong director. We Are Born Good is his first feature as director, after working as a writer on an earlier Hong Kong film. It is one of the winning projects in the College Group of the 8th First Feature Film Initiative and received HK$5 million in support from the Hong Kong Film Development Fund, and it earned nine nominations at the 63rd Golden Horse Awards, the most for any Hong Kong film that year.
highlights: Yeung Leung Chuen's first feature as director, a College Group project of the 8th First Feature Film Initiative.
A cycle of revenge set off by a wrong food order, told with black humour.
Led by Yeung Wai Lun and Chung Suet Ying, with a supporting cast that includes Hong Kong veterans.
Nine nominations at the 63rd Golden Horse Awards, including Best Feature Film and Best New Director.
gr26-046.st:
The director says the idea came from a closed-circuit television clip he saw online, in which a woman running a vegetable stall and a man buying vegetables quarrel after a minor bump and end up grappling with each other. He wondered why two people would explode over something so small, so he started from an everyday city incident, a wrong food order, and wrote two people pressed down by life.

After finishing the script, he first thought of Yeung Wai Lun for the male lead, seeing a streetwise quality in him, a slightly rough look that is also delicate underneath. Chung Suet Ying was cast because the real-life reactions she shared with him showed him the character. The film had its world premiere in the Discovery section of the 51st Toronto International Film Festival in September 2026, then its Asian premiere at the Pingyao International Film Festival, and opened in Hong Kong on 29 October.

gr26-047.title: Dead End
gr26-047.syn: An unresolved crime draws several lives together, gradually revealing hidden wounds and secrets beneath everyday existence.
gr26-047.bio: Isabella Lam directed her first dramatic feature, Dead End, and it was selected for the Vision-Asia competition at the Busan International Film Festival. highlights: Isabella Lam's first dramatic feature, with its world premiere in the Busan Vision-Asia competition.
A College Group winner of the 7th First Feature Film Initiative, produced by Soi Cheang.
Starring Lokman Yeung, built around an old case of a father's fatal fall.
A case ruled a suicide opens onto unspoken family secrets.
gr26-047.st:
The story centres on Zheng Kaiwen, a thirty-year-old programmer who lives quietly with his wife and daughter but is anxious about the future. One day a teenager named Yue appears, claiming to be his half-brother, and insists on finding out how their father fell to his death more than ten years ago. The case had many doubts and Kaiwen's mother He Meijun was once a key suspect, but it was ruled a suicide in the end.

As Yue presses on, long-buried family secrets surface, and Kaiwen has to face his father's death again and the unresolved knot with his mother. The film had its world premiere at the 31st Busan International Film Festival in October 2026.

gr26-048.title: Oasis
gr26-048.syn: After a threatening video unsettles their school, three outsiders retreat to a forest in search of belonging.
gr26-048.bio: Jannis Lenz studied at the Film Academy Vienna, where he was mentored by Jessica Hausner and worked as an assistant to Michael Haneke. His background in parkour and freerunning shaped early work such as ZERO-G, which looks at bodies in urban space, and his films move between documentary and fiction. His short Wannabe (2017) won a Prix at Clermont-Ferrand and was nominated for a European Film Award; the documentary Soldat Ahmet (2021), his master's thesis film, premiered at Visions du Réel. Oasis is his first narrative feature, premiering in Venice's Orizzonti section in 2026.
highlights: World premiere in Venice Orizzonti; Lenz's first narrative feature.
A viral video sparks panic at school and three teenagers retreat to a forest.
The woods are deforested and hold bunker and tank ruins, undermining the idea of pure refuge.
A former parkour athlete and Haneke's assistant, Lenz puts the body and silence at the centre.
gr26-048.st:
Lenz co-wrote the film with Alexander Dirninger; it is a German-Austrian co-production sold by Totem Films and had its world premiere in Venice's Orizzonti section in September 2026. It begins with a viral video of a student threatening classmates, after which the school spirals into escalating fear and violence. Under pressure from teachers and parents, three outcasts retreat into a nearby forest, where play hardens into ritual and pain becomes a release.

According to the production notes, Lenz spent much of his own childhood in the woods; when he returned there years later with his own children, the memories and images came flooding back, and he realised the idea was big enough for a feature. The forest in the film is no pure refuge: it has largely been deforested and is dotted with the ruins of bunkers and tanks, a deliberate challenge to the idea of nature as untouched sanctuary, and the film's formal choices grow out of it.

Critics describe it as asking what it means to be young in a world where behaviour is constantly under the microscope, with social media as the catalyst, and note that it is more restrained than comparable teen-violence dramas in how much it shows.
honors: 入选｜2026 Golden Rooster Film Screening · 此刻：国际新片展映
gr26-048.editorial: A slow-burning ensemble about teenagers, best for viewers willing to sit with discomfort and ask how violence is learned and seen. Notice how much space parents, teachers and phone screens take up around the three protagonists.
gr26-048.contentNote: Available story information indicates: Distress or pressure affecting children. Detailed depiction and intensity have not been verified; consider your individual needs.

gr26-049.title: The Chinese Feast
gr26-049.syn: An aspiring cook joins a restaurant facing a culinary showdown and helps recruit a retired master chef.
gr26-049.bio: Tsui Hark is a Hong Kong director and producer who founded Film Workshop with Nansun Shi in 1984 and brought wuxia and special effects into commercial cinema with Zu: Warriors from the Magic Mountain, the Once Upon a Time in China series and New Dragon Gate Inn. He co-wrote, produced and directed The Chinese Feast, a rare contemporary-set film after his 1992 The Master.
highlights: A Lunar New Year comedy that turns a cooking contest into a martial arts showdown.
Starring Leslie Cheung and Anita Yuen; Tsui Hark co-wrote, produced and directed.
The Manchu–Han Imperial Feast preparation, full of fantasy and food close-ups.
Grossed about HK$31 million, both a critical and commercial success.
gr26-049.st:
Released in the 1995 Lunar New Year season and made by Film Workshop, the film was written by Philip Cheng, Ng Man-fai, Tsui Hark and Yuen Kai-chi, shot by Peter Pau and Poon Hang-sang, scored by Lowell Lo and edited by Marco Mak. M+'s programme notes say four Lunar New Year films were released that year, with Stephen Chow's two-part A Chinese Odyssey lukewarmly received while Tsui's film was a critical and commercial success; he turns a cooking contest into a martial arts showdown and the restaurant industry into rival wuxia sects, with the Manchu–Han Imperial Feast preparation full of fantasy. It grossed about HK$31 million.

The plot begins with a young man who wants to become a chef in Canada; in the course of seeking a retired master and preparing for the Manchu–Han Imperial Feast he meets a quirky young woman (Anita Yuen). Leslie Cheung plays the young cook, with Anita Yuen. The Austin Chronicle called it Tsui Hark's loosest, most improvisational film in years, giving up the tightly symmetrical structures of Green Snake and The Lovers for an easygoing style.
honors: 入选｜2026 Golden Rooster Film Screening · 功夫·功夫：华语经典展映
gr26-049.editorial: A light Lunar New Year comedy that will make you hungry by the cooking showdown; loosely paced but packed with gags.
gr26-049.contentNote: Available story information indicates: Food preparation; Social or professional pressure. Detailed depiction and intensity have not been verified; consider your individual needs.

gr26-050.title: Beloved
gr26-050.syn: A sailor and his beloved begin a family in coastal Norway, but his repeated departures test their relationship.
gr26-050.bio: Erik Poppe was born in Norway on 24 June 1960 and worked as a conflict photographer before directing, an experience that fed into his later films. His credits include The King's Choice, about Norway's royal family in the Second World War, Utøya: July 22, which recreates the 2011 attack in a single take, and The Emigrants. In 2014 he won the Amanda Award for Best Film, becoming the first director to have every feature nominated for Best Film or Best Director. He is also co-owner of Paradox Film and the Paradox group.
highlights: Jon Fosse's first film script, written in 1998 and filmed in 2026.
First collaboration between Poppe and Fosse; opening film in Haugesund, August 2026.
The distance between a sailor and his wife is the film's recurring question.
A Danish-Norwegian-Swedish co-production.
gr26-050.st:
Beloved (Norwegian title Kjærast) is based on an original screenplay by Nobel laureate Jon Fosse, the first film script he wrote. According to Poppe in 2025, Fosse wrote it in 1998 and for more than two decades only the two of them knew it existed; he described a story of passion and emotion that also asks how much distance love can endure.

A Danish-Norwegian-Swedish co-production starring Leo de la Nuez and Kristi-Helene Engberg, it opened the Norwegian International Film Festival in Haugesund in August 2026 and was released in Norway in September. At the premiere Poppe said that where much on screen shows cynicism and distance, the most radical thing may be to tell stories about closeness and hope.

Fosse's language is known for brevity, repetition and silence, which is hard to put on screen. Norwegian reviews are divided: some feel landscape, stillness and glances make the unspoken almost tangible, while others find the direction lacking a distinct personality.
honors: 入选｜2026 Golden Rooster Film Screening · 此刻：国际新片展映
gr26-050.editorial: Quiet and sparing with words; love is carried by silence, the sea and glances. Fosse readers will find it easier to enter, but it also works as a seaside fable about leaving and waiting.
gr26-050.contentNote: Available story information indicates: Relationship conflict or coercion; Ageing and care. Detailed depiction and intensity have not been verified; consider your individual needs.

gr26-051.title: Everything Else is Noise
gr26-051.syn: A composer's television interview unravels through awkward questions, technical mishaps and unexpected interruptions, exposing artistic vanity and sexism.
gr26-051.bio: Nicolás Pereda, born in 1982, is a Mexican director who combines fiction and documentary techniques to explore the everyday. His work has been shown at festivals including Cannes, Berlin and Venice, in more than 30 retrospectives, and in museums such as the Reina Sofía and MoMA. Recent films include Fauna (2020), Lázaro de noche (2024) and Cobre (2025). Everything Else Is Noise (Lo demás es ruido) is his 2026 film, which he also shot and edited, re-teaming with actress Teresita Sánchez.
highlights: World premiere in the Berlinale Forum; a 71-minute chamber comedy.
A TV interview interrupted again and again by equipment failures, a barking dog and unexpected visitors.
An absurd send-up of artistic vanity and gender prejudice, with a thread of melancholy.
Pereda shot and edited it himself, re-teaming with Teresita Sánchez.
gr26-051.st:
The film had its world premiere in the Berlinale Forum on 14 February 2026; it runs 71 minutes and is a Mexico-Germany-Canada co-production. Musician and composer Tere (Teresita Sánchez) opens her home to a friend's television interview; the conversation meanders and new voices drift in: equipment fails, a dog barks, an unexpected visitor arrives, and a supposedly professional interview slowly becomes an absurd stage for artistic vanity and gender prejudice.

AFI Silver describes Tere as an established musician who never quite got the recognition she deserved, always in the shadow of male colleagues; the film gleefully skewers avant-garde musicians, filmmakers and especially the male ego. The Forum describes a minimalist, absurdly comic chamber piece proving that the extraordinary hides in the everyday, and that noise and music are inseparable.

Pereda co-wrote it with Juan Francisco Maldonado; the music is by Violeta García. It later played the Toronto and New York film festivals.
gr26-051.editorial: It is short, and the humour comes from dialogue and awkward pauses; no knowledge of Mexico's art scene is required. Notice how the word 'noise' keeps shifting: it is an interruption, and also another form of expression.
gr26-051.contentNote: Available story information indicates: Discrimination or abuse of power; Social inequality or workplace mistreatment. Detailed depiction and intensity have not been verified; consider your individual needs.

gr26-052.title: Full Phil
gr26-052.syn: An American businessman brings his daughter to Paris to repair their relationship, only for the carefully planned trip to spiral into absurdity.
gr26-052.bio: Quentin Dupieux was born in Paris in 1974; he is a French director, writer, cinematographer and editor, and also a musician under the name Mr. Oizo. Known for absurdist comedy, his films include Rubber (2010), Deerskin (2019), Mandibles and Yannick, which typically build a short film on a single minimalist absurd premise. Full Phil is one of two films he had at Cannes this year (the other is Vertiginous, his first fully animated feature, which closed the Directors' Fortnight) and his first English-language film in about a decade.
highlights: Cannes Midnight Screenings: a 78-minute absurdist comedy written, shot and edited by Dupieux himself.
Woody Harrelson and Kristen Stewart play an estranged father and daughter trying to 'repair' things by eating in a luxury Paris hotel.
Phil's belly grows with whatever his daughter eats: an absurd, concrete countdown that pushes the film out of control.
Dupieux's first English-language film in about a decade; he calls it 'Emily in Paris in hell'.
gr26-052.st:
Full Phil premiered on 17 May 2026 in the out-of-competition Midnight Screenings at Cannes. Dupieux wrote, shot and edited it himself; it is a France-Belgium-Luxembourg co-production with StudioCanal handling international sales, and it runs 78 minutes. He told Variety it is like 'Emily in Paris in hell, a fever dream, a nightmare version of it'.

Wealthy American tycoon Phil Doom (Woody Harrelson) takes his estranged daughter Madeleine (Kristen Stewart) to a luxury Paris hotel to rebuild their relationship. They eat gluttonously, and the more Madeleine eats the bigger Phil's stomach grows, a ticking-clock device that carries the film to its end. A hotel employee (Charlotte Le Bon) refuses to let Phil out of her sight because he raised his voice slightly at his daughter. Cineuropa notes that Dupieux delves seriously and sincerely into the Dooms' troubled family history, a newer slant for him.

Critics are sharply divided: Eye for Film gave it 3.5 stars and thought it could be a gateway to his back catalogue for English-language audiences, while Roger Ebert and the Harvard Crimson found it hollow, with unpleasant characters.
gr26-052.editorial: If you'd like to try Dupieux but fear he's too strange, this one has big stars and a short running time, so it works as an introduction. The humour is cold and critics are split; keep expectations moderate and take it as a fable about anger and reconciliation.
gr26-052.contentNote: Available story information indicates: Excessive eating; Family conflict or separation; Horror or threat. Detailed depiction and intensity have not been verified; consider your individual needs.

gr26-053.title: Queen Budapest
gr26-053.syn: Queen's 1986 Budapest concert and behind-the-scenes journey capture a shared musical moment for the band, the city and its audience.
gr26-053.bio: János Zsombolyai is a Hungarian director and cinematographer who was chosen to direct the filming of Queen's 1986 concert in Budapest. With producer George Mihály, cinematographer Elemér Ragályi and nearly twenty camera operators, he captured the show on 35mm film; it is his best-known work.
highlights: Népstadion, Budapest, 27 July 1986: about 80,000 fans on the Magic Tour.
Hungary's state studio requisitioned 17 national 35mm cameras and shot in widescreen.
Live footage from Freddie Mercury's last tour with the band.
Remixed in 2012 from the original multitracks.
gr26-053.st:
On 27 July 1986 Queen played the Népstadion in Budapest as part of the Magic Tour, the last tour with Freddie Mercury. An estimated 80,000 fans attended, and it is regarded as the first stadium concert by a Western rock band behind the Iron Curtain, three years before it fell.

The Hungarian authorities and film industry took it seriously: the state studio MaFilm requisitioned all 17 available 35mm cameras in the country and brought together some of its best cinematographers, including Elemér Ragályi and Lajos Koltai, shooting in widescreen and from a helicopter. The film opens with a long introduction to the city of Budapest before the concert itself takes over.

It was released on video in early 1987 and remixed and restored from the original multitracks in 2012 for DVD and Blu-ray, with some cinema screenings; Queen: Budapest is the title used for the later ultra-high-definition edition.
honors: 入选｜2026 Golden Rooster Film Screening · 回声：国际经典展映
gr26-053.editorial: If you want a complete Queen concert on the big screen, this is it; it is also an archive of Eastern Europe near the end of the Cold War. The cinema mix is loud, so be mindful if you are sensitive to volume.
gr26-053.contentNote: The available synopsis has been reviewed, but no specific sensitive content has been established. This is not an all-ages assurance or a full content assessment.

gr26-054.title: Edward Scissorhands
gr26-054.syn: An unfinished artificial man with scissors for hands enters suburban life, where his talents inspire affection, jealousy and fear.
gr26-054.bio: Tim Burton grew up in Burbank, California, and began as an animator; his short Vincent (1982) was narrated by his childhood idol Vincent Price, and the two became close. After Pee-wee's Big Adventure, Beetlejuice and Batman, Edward Scissorhands was his fourth collaboration with composer Danny Elfman, and both consider it among their most personal work.
highlights: Conceived by Burton and Thompson; Thompson called the script a love poem to Burton.
Vincent Price's last major role.
Danny Elfman's score; the fourth Burton-Elfman collaboration.
Oscar nomination for Best Makeup; pastel suburbia shot in Lakeland.
gr26-054.st:
The film grew from Burton's feelings about his suburban Burbank childhood and his drawings of a figure with scissors for hands. According to the AFI Catalog the project dates to 1986, and Burton first imagined it as a musical; he showed the sketches to writer Caroline Thompson and hired her during pre-production on Beetlejuice. Warner Bros. passed; 20th Century Fox agreed to finance a script without interfering, with four weeks after delivery to green-light it or the rights would revert to Burton. Thompson has described the script as a love poem to him.

Johnny Depp has said he was hooked by Burton's drawings rather than the script; Vincent Price plays the Inventor in his last major role released in his lifetime. It was shot in Lakeland, Florida, from March to June 1990, with production design by Bo Welch and makeup by Stan Winston and Ve Neill, which earned an Oscar nomination for Best Makeup; it was released in December 1990.

Elfman's score and Burton's gothic suburban fairy tale together became the clearest statement of the 'Burton style'.
honors: 入选｜2026 Golden Rooster Film Screening · 回声：国际经典展映
gr26-054.editorial: A modern fairy tale about tenderness that is not accepted, good for families, couples or a rewatch. Notice the candy colours of the suburb against the black-and-white of the castle.
gr26-054.contentNote: Available story information indicates: Exclusion or prejudice; Violence or injury; Emotional distress or trauma. Detailed depiction and intensity have not been verified; consider your individual needs.

gr26-055.title: No Country for Old Men
gr26-055.syn: A hunter takes cash from a failed drug deal and becomes a killer's target, while an ageing sheriff follows the violence.
gr26-055.bio: Joel and Ethan Coen were born in Minnesota and have long written, directed and edited together, crediting their editing under the pseudonym Roderick Jaynes. No Country for Old Men was their first adaptation of Cormac McCarthy and remains their only Best Picture winner; following a few less-celebrated films, many regard it as their signature work.
highlights: The Coens' only Best Picture winner, plus Director, Adapted Screenplay and Javier Bardem's Best Supporting Actor.
Adapted from Cormac McCarthy's 2005 novel.
Long stretches have almost no dialogue or music.
Cinematography by Roger Deakins, music by Carter Burwell.
gr26-055.st:
Producer Scott Rudin bought the rights to McCarthy's novel and suggested the Coens, who at the time were trying to adapt James Dickey's To the White Sea. According to the Los Angeles Times, one of the things that drew them was McCarthy's tendency to subvert genre. Ethan said they had no contact with McCarthy while writing and only in contact during filming.

Shot in Texas and New Mexico in 2006, with Roger Deakins behind the camera and Carter Burwell's music, the film names the pharmacy robbed by Chigurh after the Coens' own company, Mike Zoss Productions, itself named for a Minneapolis drugstore they frequented as boys. It premiered in competition at Cannes in May 2007 and then played Toronto and New York.

It earned eight Oscar nominations and won four: Best Picture, Best Director, Best Adapted Screenplay and Best Supporting Actor for Javier Bardem. Its budget was about $25 million and it grossed about $171 million worldwide.
gr26-055.editorial: A quiet crime western with sudden violence. Do not expect a conventional chase-and-showdown arc; the film leaves incomprehensible violence for the audience to digest. It contains violence; check the content notes.
gr26-055.contentNote: Available story information indicates: Violence and bloody injury; Drug-related themes. Detailed depiction and intensity have not been verified; consider your individual needs.

gr26-056.title: The Return
gr26-056.syn: An absent father returns to take his two sons on an unsettling journey to a remote island.
gr26-056.bio: Andrey Zvyagintsev was born in Novosibirsk in 1964. The Return, his first feature, won the Golden Lion at Venice in 2003 together with the prize for best first film, and was seen as a major return of Russian cinema to the international stage after Tarkovsky. He went on to make The Banishment, Elena and Leviathan.
highlights: Golden Lion and best first film at Venice, Zvyagintsev's debut feature.
A father absent for twelve years takes his two sons to an island on a lake.
Vladimir Garin, who played the elder brother, drowned shortly before the premiere.
European Film Awards 'Discovery of the Year'.
gr26-056.st:
The film was written by Vladimir Moiseyenko and Aleksandr Novototsky, shot by Mikhail Krichman and produced by REN Film with Dmitry Lesnevsky. A father returns after twelve years away and takes his two sons, 15-year-old Andrei and 12-year-old Ivan, to a remote island on a lake; the closing photographs show no father, so there is no proof of what the trip contained.

The director has said they spent half a year looking for the boys and in the end found 'two genius kids'. On 6 September 2003 the film won the Golden Lion at the 60th Venice festival, but Vladimir Garin, who played the elder brother, had drowned at 16 two months before the premiere, and Zvyagintsev dedicated the Lion to him.

Critics linked it to Tarkovsky, whose Ivan's Childhood had also won the Venice Golden Lion in 1962.
gr26-056.editorial: A quiet, oppressive coming-of-age parable with a slow pace and plenty of silence, best for viewers willing to read it as a metaphor about fathers, authority and trust. The ending is heavy.
gr26-056.contentNote: Available story information indicates: Discrimination or abuse of power; Distress or pressure affecting children; Family conflict or separation. Detailed depiction and intensity have not been verified; consider your individual needs.

gr26-057.title: The Meltdown
gr26-057.syn: In 1992, a nine-year-old befriends a German athlete at her grandparents' ski lodge before a disappearance exposes adult secrets.
gr26-057.bio: Manuela Martelli was born in Santiago on 16 April 1983 and began as an actor before turning to directing. Her first feature, Chile '76, played in Cannes' Directors' Fortnight in 2022, a Hitchcockian account of a bourgeois housewife's political awakening under dictatorship. The Meltdown (El deshielo) is her second feature, selected for Un Certain Regard at Cannes in 2026 and sold internationally by Les Films du Losange.
highlights: Selected for Un Certain Regard at Cannes; Martelli's second feature after Chile '76.
Chile in 1992, just after the dictatorship: an iceberg shown at the Expo stands for a country wanting to turn a page.
A nine-year-old's point of view: after her German friend disappears, the adults' silence and mutual protection slowly surface.
Divided reviews: praised for atmosphere and form, criticised by some as too oblique.
gr26-057.st:
The film had its world premiere in Un Certain Regard on 14 May 2026. It is set in Chile in 1992, not long after Pinochet's dictatorship. Nine-year-old Inés (Maya O'Rourke) is left behind when her parents go to the Seville Expo, where that year's Chilean pavilion showed an iceberg; she stays at her grandparents' hotel at the foot of an Andean ski resort and befriends Hanna, a fifteen-year-old German skier. When Hanna suddenly disappears, Inés becomes almost the only witness and gradually senses the silence and mutual protection among the adults around her.

Critics are divided. Screen Daily reads the child's loss of innocence as an allegory for Chile's reckoning in the post-Pinochet era; Cineuropa calls it subtle, allusive and atmospheric; Variety finds the director's poise impressive but the whole less than the sum of its parts. Some viewers found it too opaque.

The Meltdown continues Chile '76's interest in the culture of silence after the transition to democracy, working through atmosphere and omission rather than direct confrontation. It opened in Chile on 3 September 2026.
gr26-057.editorial: A film driven by atmosphere and omission; the point is less solving the mystery than watching a child grow up inside silence. Viewers wanting clear answers may feel short-changed. A little background on Chile in 1992, just after the dictatorship, helps.
gr26-057.contentNote: Available story information indicates: Missing loved ones; Distress or pressure affecting children; Crime, threat or interpersonal conflict. Detailed depiction and intensity have not been verified; consider your individual needs.

gr26-058.title: Goodbye South, Goodbye
gr26-058.syn: A man and his young companions pursue elusive business opportunities across Taiwan, caught between family, friendship and an uncertain future.
gr26-058.bio: Hou Hsiao-hsien is a leading director of Taiwan New Cinema, known for long takes and static camera positions, with works such as A City of Sadness, The Puppetmaster and Good Men, Good Women drawing on history or personal memory. Goodbye South, Goodbye was the first film set in the present day since 1987's Daughter of the Nile.
highlights: In the 1996 Cannes competition; Hou's first contemporary-set film since 1987.
Written by Chu T'ien-wen, starring Jack Kao, Lim Giong and Annie Shizuka Inoh.
A Taiwan–Japan (Shochiku) co-production.
Cahiers du cinéma once named it among the best films of the 1990s.
gr26-058.st:
Written by Chu T'ien-wen from a story by Jack Kao and King Jieh-wen, the film was produced by Hou's 3H Films with Japan's Shochiku as a Taiwan–Japan co-production. Jack Kao plays Gao, Lim Giong plays Flat Head, and Annie Shizuka Inoh plays Pretzel, with Lim also providing music. A group of small-time Taipei hoodlums hope to change their lives through business schemes: Gao plans to go to Shanghai to open a nightclub with a friend, while his girlfriend Ying wants him to stay in Taiwan and open a restaurant.

It premiered in the official competition at Cannes on 12 May 1996, the year the Palme d'Or went to Secrets & Lies. Sources give running times from 107 to 124 minutes. Cahiers du cinéma later named it, with The Bridges of Madison County and Carlito's Way, the best film of the 1990s.

Hou had seldom filmed present-day stories before; here he observes the paradoxical effects of modernisation on Taiwan, with characters who have neither a past nor a clear future.
honors: 入选｜2026 Golden Rooster Film Screening · 功夫·功夫：华语经典展映
gr26-058.editorial: Hou's long takes and open spaces, watching a group of drifters wander between southern Taiwan and Shanghai; slow-paced, for patient viewers.
gr26-058.contentNote: Available story information indicates: Violence or injury; Family conflict or separation. Detailed depiction and intensity have not been verified; consider your individual needs.
