gr26-059.title: What Belongs to Others
gr26-059.syn: A burglar finds a dead homeowner and impersonates his partner, imagining a different life through his relationships.
gr26-059.bio: Grzegorz Dębowski is a Polish director and screenwriter. His first feature, Next to Nothing (2023), like this film, revolves around a dead body and focuses on people living on the margins of Polish society. Cineuropa says he combines social-realist aesthetics with crime-story propulsion and uses genre and catharsis to fashion a more audience-friendly form of social cinema. This is his second feature; it played in the Orizzonti competition of the 83rd Venice Film Festival and won the Grand Prix at the Warsaw International Film Festival.
highlights: Premiered in Venice Orizzonti, then won the Warsaw Grand Prix; the director's second feature, again built around a dead body.
Kasia breaks into a stranger's home and starts using his identity to piece together a life of her own; the line between 'owning' and 'stealing' blurs.
Observational social-realist imagery with thriller suspense about whether she will be exposed.
The jury praised a non-judgmental portrait of a flawed, elusive woman; Ewa Pająk's memory-losing older woman is unforgettable.
gr26-059.st:
What Belongs to Others (Polish title Cudze rzeczy) had its world premiere in September 2026 in the Venice Orizzonti section. It begins with a burglary: Kasia (Monika Sabina Kwiatkowska) and her boyfriend Darek, who pose as cleaners to break into apartments, have not paid their rent. During one job she finds the body of Piotr, a man who died alone; after her boyfriend is arrested, she returns to the dead man's flat, poses as his partner and starts piecing together his life, finances and family. Critics note how little the film tells us about Kasia herself and how little dialogue there is, which makes Kwiatkowska's performance especially important.

In October it won the Warsaw Grand Prix at the 42nd Warsaw International Film Festival, worth PLN 120,000. The jury praised its precise and delicate storytelling, exceptional performances and a complex portrait, devoid of judgment, of a flawed and elusive woman who, slipping into a stranger's identity and life, finds the possibility of her own. Reviewers also single out Ewa Pająk as an older woman losing her memory, and loneliness as the film's running theme.
gr26-059.editorial: For viewers who like social realism with a touch of suspense. Notice that the film barely explains Kasia's past yet shows through every small gesture in the dead man's home what she lacks; and consider what the title's 'what belongs to others' really refers to.
gr26-059.contentNote: Available story information indicates: Crime, threat or interpersonal conflict; Discovery of a dead person; Relationship conflict or coercion. Detailed depiction and intensity have not been verified; consider your individual needs.

gr26-060.title: Black Money for White Nights
gr26-060.syn: A Bulgarian couple's dream trip is derailed by war and a travel scam, forcing them to confront money and marital deception.
gr26-060.bio: Kristina Grozeva (born in Sofia) and Petar Valchanov (born in Plovdiv) are long-time creative and life partners. Their short Jump (2012) was nominated for a European Film Award; after their feature debut Glory (2016), The Father (2019) won the Crystal Globe at Karlovy Vary, and Triumph, starring Maria Bakalova, became their third film chosen as Bulgaria's Oscar submission. Black Money for White Nights is their fifth feature and returned them to the Karlovy Vary Crystal Globe competition.
highlights: Crystal Globe competition; world premiere July 2026; the duo's fifth feature.
An older couple save petty bribes for a St Petersburg trip to see the White Nights.
War and a scam wreck the journey and old lies in the marriage surface.
Edited by Yorgos Mavropsaridis, a long-time Lanthimos collaborator.
gr26-060.st:
The film had its world premiere in the Crystal Globe competition at Karlovy Vary in July 2026. Grozeva and Valchanov wrote it with Decho Taralezhkov; Yorgos Mavropsaridis, the editor long associated with Yorgos Lanthimos, cut it, and it is a Bulgarian-Greek co-production. Marina, a sixty-year-old maternity nurse, and her husband Gosha, a railway employee, have for years saved money from petty bribes for a trip to St Petersburg to see the White Nights, and for Marina to visit her father's grave. When the war in Ukraine begins in early 2022 and a scam hits, the couple are stranded in Sofia and fall back on Marina's sister.

Critics see it as another darkly comic dissection of corruption in Bulgaria: the gags are gentle ironies, mostly visual, and the directors do not laugh at their protagonists but treat them as cogs in a system. Variety found it more audience-friendly than their previous feature Triumph, with the real drama in the cracks of a long, childless marriage that open once the scam is exposed.

Some reviewers note that unexpected cruelty sits awkwardly with the satirical tone and that the ending is bleak.
honors: 入选｜2026 Golden Rooster Film Screening · 此刻：国际新片展映
gr26-060.editorial: Dry humour and social critique run side by side; you will laugh, but not comfortably. Watch the small moments where the couple know something is wrong and do it anyway; that is where the film's weight lies.
warnings: War, conflict or threat of war
gr26-060.contentNote: Available story information indicates: Financial hardship or exploitation; War, conflict or threat of war; Relationship conflict or coercion. Detailed depiction and intensity have not been verified; consider your individual needs.

gr26-061.title: Ah Fei
gr26-061.syn: A daughter looks back at her mother's sacrifices and her own upbringing as two generations seek choices beyond patriarchal expectations.
gr26-061.bio: Wan Jen is a Taiwan New Cinema director who took part in the 1983 omnibus The Sandwich Man and later made Super Citizen Ko, among other works. Ah Fei (Oil Hemp Seeds) adapts Liao Hui-ying's novel of the same name and is one of the earlier Taiwan New Cinema films centred on women's circumstances.
highlights: Adapted from Liao Hui-ying's novel; the screenplay won a Golden Horse for best adaptation.
From countryside to a Taipei slum to a city-centre flat: the changes across two generations of mother and daughter.
One of the earlier Taiwan New Cinema films to centre women's circumstances.
Recently digitally restored and re-released.
gr26-061.st:
The film adapts Liao Hui-ying's 1983 novel of the same name, and Liao and Hou Hsiao-hsien won a Golden Horse for best adapted screenplay. Liao is known for writing about disadvantaged families and rapid social change, especially as Taiwan's economy took off in the 1970s; the book is autobiographical, about a postwar generation of women growing up in hardship. The Taipei Times notes that in the early 1980s the government's grip on society was loosening, social movements were taking root, and in 1982 the Awakening Foundation was founded as Taiwan's first NGO explicitly committed to promoting gender equality.

The film follows Ah Fei and her mother Hsin-chin from the countryside to a Taipei slum and then to a well-appointed city-centre flat, two generations of women reflected against patriarchy, marriage and changes in education; one critic reads Ah Fei's liberation as that of her generation and as a reconciliation within cycles of patriarchal entitlement, male failure and internalised misogyny. It has recently been digitally restored and distributed by Era International.
honors: 入选｜2026 Golden Rooster Film Screening · 功夫·功夫：华语经典展映
gr26-061.editorial: A Taiwan New Cinema film about mother–daughter relations and women's circumstances; plain in pace and delicate in feeling, for viewers interested in 1980s Taiwanese social change.
gr26-061.contentNote: Available story information indicates: Discrimination or abuse of power; Relationship conflict or coercion. Detailed depiction and intensity have not been verified; consider your individual needs.

gr26-062.title: Drunken Master
gr26-062.syn: A mischievous young Wong Fei-hung learns an eccentric martial art from a seemingly disreputable master.
gr26-062.bio: Yuen Woo-ping comes from a martial arts family, and Drunken Master was his second collaboration with Jackie Chan after Snake in the Eagle's Shadow. He later designed fights for The Matrix and Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon in Hollywood; his father Yuen Siu-tien plays Beggar So in the film, his last film released in his lifetime.
highlights: Jackie Chan and Yuen Woo-ping's second collaboration, which established the kung fu comedy genre.
Yuen Siu-tien plays Beggar So in his last film released in his lifetime.
The Eight Drunken Immortals forms were devised by Yuen Woo-ping.
Its theme song is drawn from the folk song Under the General's Orders.
gr26-062.st:
Released in October 1978, the film was produced and co-written by Ng See-yuen for Seasonal Film Corporation, with Golden Harvest co-distributing; cinematography is by Chang Hui and music by Chow Fu-liang. It used much the same crew as Snake in the Eagle's Shadow earlier that year, including Jackie Chan, Yuen Siu-tien and Hwang Jang-lee, and though the stories are unrelated, they are similar in structure.

It presents Chan and Yuen Siu-tien as fictionalised versions of Wong Fei-hung and Beggar So: the mischievous young Wong is forced to train under the fierce master of drunken fighting. The 'Eight Drunken Immortals' forms are thought to be the invention of Yuen Woo-ping, based on routines from other styles; the theme song comes from the folk song Under the General's Orders, which has since been associated with Wong Fei-hung. In Hong Kong it earned about two and a half times the box office of Snake in the Eagle's Shadow, and helped create the kung fu comedy genre, with Chan its leading star.

A sequel, Drunken Master II, was directed by Lau Kar-leung in 1994, with Chan again as Wong Fei-hung.
honors: 入选｜2026 Golden Rooster Film Screening · 功夫·功夫：华语经典展映
gr26-062.editorial: Kung fu and comedy combined; the training scenes look gruelling but are very funny, a good entry point to Jackie Chan's early work.
gr26-062.contentNote: Available story information indicates: Violence or injury; Alcohol use. Detailed depiction and intensity have not been verified; consider your individual needs.

gr26-063.title: Blade Runner: The Final Cut
gr26-063.syn: A detective hunts escaped replicants in a future Los Angeles, questioning the boundaries of humanity, memory and identity.
gr26-063.bio: Ridley Scott, born in Britain, moved from commercials to features and made Blade Runner (1982) after Alien (1979). The Final Cut is the version he calls his definitive director's cut, released in 2007 for the film's 25th anniversary.
highlights: Scott's definitive director's cut, released in 2007 for the 25th anniversary.
Seven years of restoration led by producer Charles de Lauzirika, from 2000.
Adapted from Philip K. Dick's novel, with a score by Vangelis.
Added and extended scenes, restored effects and new 5.1 sound.
gr26-063.st:
The film adapts Philip K. Dick's novel Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?, written by Hampton Fancher and David Peoples, shot by Jordan Cronenweth and scored by Vangelis. The 1982 release exists in several cuts; a workprint screening discovered in 1990 led to the 1992 'Director's Cut', though Scott only supplied notes then and restorer Michael Arick led the work.

From 2000, restoration producer Charles de Lauzirika began working with Scott on a final, definitive version; legal and financial issues halted it in 2001 and it was completed in 2007. Scott said the Final Cut is the product of seven years of research and restoration and is his definitive director's cut. It adds extended and restored scenes, cleaned-up effects and new 5.1 audio.

It premiered at the Venice Film Festival (out of competition) in September 2007 and had a limited release in New York and Los Angeles in October, alongside the documentary Dangerous Days: Making Blade Runner.
honors: 入选｜2026 Golden Rooster Film Screening · 回声：国际经典展映
gr26-063.editorial: If you watch only one version of Blade Runner, make it this one. Notice how images such as the unicorn and memory change your view of Deckard; many questions in the film have no fixed answer.
gr26-063.contentNote: Available story information indicates: Violence or injury; Death and bereavement. Detailed depiction and intensity have not been verified; consider your individual needs.

gr26-064.title: We Are All Strangers
gr26-064.syn: A young man and his father navigate love and financial pressure in Singapore as unexpected changes reshape their family.
gr26-064.bio: Anthony Chen is a Singaporean director who wrote, directed and produced We Are All Strangers, the last film in his Growing Up trilogy after Ilo Ilo (2013) and Wet Season (2019). The first two films reportedly won more than 50 international awards between them, including five Golden Horse awards. This is also the first Singaporean film in the main competition of the Berlin International Film Festival.
highlights: The final film of the Growing Up trilogy and the first Singaporean film in the Berlinale main competition.
Yeo Yann Yann and Koh Jia Ler work with Anthony Chen for the third time.
Seven nominations at the 63rd Golden Horse Awards, including Best Feature Film and Best Director.
Singapore's submission for the Oscar for Best International Feature.
gr26-064.st:
The film is set in present-day Singapore and spans three years. Twenty-one-year-old Junyang enjoys the freedom of youth while his father struggles to keep up their modest life. An unexpected turn in Junyang's relationship with his girlfriend changes their lives completely, and a lively woman enters his father's life and quietly shifts the fragile balance between father and son. Reviewers note that the film is dedicated to the director's own family.

Chen worked with Yeo Yann Yann and Koh Jia Ler for the third time. Koh has had many jobs in real life, including working in bars, selling phone accessories, delivering parcels and doing airport pick-ups, and these experiences were written into Junyang's story. Chen says not everything was planned in advance, as reality kept developing. The film is in Hokkien, Mandarin and English, runs 157 minutes, and was chosen as Singapore's submission for the Oscar for Best International Feature.
honors: 入选｜2026 Golden Rooster Film Screening · 拾光：华语新片展映
gr26-064.editorial: A 157-minute family drama about how blood relatives and chosen family learn to become a family again. The pace is unhurried with touches of dark humour, and the last part brings money and debt pressure; good for viewers willing to spend time watching its characters grow up.
gr26-064.contentNote: Available story information indicates: Financial hardship or exploitation; Family conflict or separation. Detailed depiction and intensity have not been verified; consider your individual needs.

gr26-065.title: Moonage Daydream
gr26-065.syn: Music, performances, interviews and private footage form an immersive exploration of David Bowie's changing artistic identities.
gr26-065.bio: Brett Morgen is an American documentary director whose credits include The Kid Stays in the Picture, Cobain: Montage of Heck and Jane. He last attended Cannes in 2002 with The Kid Stays in the Picture and returned twenty years later with Moonage Daydream, which he wrote, directed, produced and edited.
highlights: The first film officially sanctioned by Bowie's estate, with access to about five million archive items.
Premiered in Cannes' Midnight Screenings in 2022 after five years of work.
40 remastered songs (1970–1977), mixed in multichannel from original stems.
Written, directed, produced and edited by Brett Morgen.
gr26-065.st:
In 2017 David Bowie's estate gave Morgen unfiltered access to Bowie's archives, including all master recordings; the archive is reported to hold about five million items, including paintings, recordings, photographs and film. It became the first film officially sanctioned by the estate, and took five years to make. Morgen spent two years selecting 16mm and 35mm footage, much of it unseen; the film features 40 remastered songs from 1970 to 1977, with music producer Tony Visconti involved and a multichannel mix by Paul Massey from Bowie's original stems.

It premiered on 23 May 2022 in Cannes' Midnight Screenings (out of competition) and was released by Neon in the US on 16 September, with a focus on IMAX and Dolby Atmos. Morgen has said Bowie cannot be defined, only experienced, so he designed the film as an experience rather than a conventional biography.

The title comes from Bowie's 1972 song of the same name.
honors: 入选｜2026 Golden Rooster Film Screening · 回声：国际经典展映
gr26-065.editorial: Not a chronological biography but an immersive experience of sound and image, best in a cinema with good audio. Be mindful if you are sensitive to flashing lights or loud volume.
gr26-065.contentNote: Also informed by a published overseas content advisory. The running time and cut may differ from this screening; consider your individual needs.

gr26-066.title: The General
gr26-066.syn: During the American Civil War, a railway engineer pursues the enemy soldiers who have stolen both his locomotive and his sweetheart.
gr26-066.bio: Buster Keaton was an American silent-era comedian and director famed for his deadpan face and daring self-performed stunts; Clyde Bruckman, who co-directed The General, also co-wrote it. The General is Keaton's best-known work and is often said to have closed the peak of his career.
highlights: Based on a memoir of the Civil War locomotive chase, shot in Oregon with real locomotives.
Keaton performed all his stunts; about 500 National Guard members played the soldiers.
Among the first films selected for the US National Film Registry in 1989.
A silent film with English intertitles; the live or recorded score varies by screening.
gr26-066.st:
The story was inspired by the Great Locomotive Chase of 1862 during the American Civil War, adapted from William Pittenger's 1889 memoir The Great Locomotive Chase. In early 1926 Clyde Bruckman told Keaton about it; location manager Burt Jackson found old-fashioned narrow-gauge railways in central Oregon, where a lumber railroad owned two vintage locomotives that the production bought, and three steam locomotives were eventually used.

In May 1926 the company arrived in Cottage Grove, Oregon, with 18 freight cars of props, and shooting began in June; about 500 members of the Oregon National Guard were hired to play the Union and Confederate soldiers. Keaton performed all his own stunts, which put him in considerable danger, and the AFI notes his effort to use historically accurate locomotives, sets and costumes.

It premiered in Tokyo in late 1926 and opened in New York in February 1927 to disappointing business; in 1989 it was among the first films selected for the Library of Congress's National Film Registry, and it is now often regarded as a peak of silent comedy.
honors: 入选｜2026 Golden Rooster Film Screening · 回声：国际经典展映
gr26-066.editorial: At 79 minutes, an almost continuous chase whose laughs come from action rather than words, and a good first silent film. Notice how the train is at once prop, character and stage.
warnings: War, conflict or threat of war
gr26-066.contentNote: Available story information indicates: War, conflict or threat of war; Dangerous situations or accidents; Historical viewpoints. Detailed depiction and intensity have not been verified; consider your individual needs.

gr26-067.title: Ghost in the Cell
gr26-067.syn: Prisoners facing violence and mysterious deaths must overcome their differences to survive a supernatural force.
gr26-067.bio: Joko Anwar is an Indonesian genre filmmaker best known for the horror films Satan's Slaves and Impetigore, and also directed the superhero film Gundala. Ghost in the Cell is his twelfth feature, which he wrote, directed and edited; it had its world premiere in the Berlinale Forum in February 2026. He often uses horror and comedy to address social and political issues, and has said that horror has always had its origin in environmental and political realities.
highlights: World premiere in the Berlinale Forum; Anwar's twelfth feature.
A ghost in a fictional prison punishes those with a 'negative aura'.
Gore, slapstick, dance and political satire in one mix.
Touches on illegal mining and environmental destruction.
gr26-067.st:
The film is set in the fictional Labuan Angsana prison, billed as one of Indonesia's worst. Protagonist Anggoro (Abimana Aryasatya) is in cell block C, home to thieves, conmen and murderers. The inmates believe that newcomer Dimas is followed by a ghost that kills anyone with a negative aura. The prison has a prayer room and an arts room run by an inmate dancer, Novilham, and both dance and prayer become stopgap defences against the spirit.

In an interview with Variety, Anwar said the prison is a concentrated laboratory for social hierarchies, and the ghost does not haunt but holds people accountable; he writes issues such as illegal mining and environmental destruction into the horror, and said Forum is a section where films can be uncomfortable and unresolved.

After its Berlin premiere in February 2026 it played festivals including FrightFest in the UK. Reviews describe a mix of gore, slapstick, action and political satire with bold primary colours, in which laughter often sticks in the throat.
gr26-067.editorial: An unrestrained genre film with high levels of both laughs and gore, best for viewers who can take the blood and who read the laughter as a reaction to reality. Check the content notes if you are sensitive to graphic horror.
gr26-067.contentNote: Available story information indicates: Violence or injury; Horror or threat; Death and bereavement. Detailed depiction and intensity have not been verified; consider your individual needs.

gr26-068.title: Backstage Madness
gr26-068.syn: An ageing director's artistic ambitions collide with producers, investors and family pressures in an increasingly chaotic production.
gr26-068.bio: Amanbek Azhymat was born in 1990 in Naryn, Kyrgyzstan, and in 2013 studied under director Temir Birnazarov. He worked as a film editor and cinematographer; his documentary The PE Teacher, Gold and the River (2014) won the Grand Prix at the Bastau International Film Festival, and his short Warrior (2022) is about the absurdity of war. Backstage Madness is his first feature, premiering in the First Feature Competition at Tallinn Black Nights in November 2025 and later playing Fantasia in 2026.
highlights: Premiered in Tallinn Black Nights' First Feature Competition, November 2025; a debut from Kyrgyzstan.
A 70-year-old writer versus a commercial producer, with film-within-film and reality intertwined.
Tarantino-inspired visuals mixed with musical numbers and absurd comedy.
One lead is a non-professional actor, the other a pop singer.
gr26-068.st:
Azhymat co-wrote the film with Zhanysh Dadabaev. Its hero is a nameless 70-year-old screenwriter (non-professional actor Bolot Tileberdiev) who still types on an old typewriter and tries to keep his artistic ideals, while his nephew, a producer played by pop singer Kuralbek Chokoev, wants a Hollywood-style film with gunfights, explosions and love scenes, and investors keep demanding to be written in as leads.

According to Fantasia, Azhymat drew on years as an editor and cinematographer, seeing the darkness beneath the film industry's glamour, and on Quentin Tarantino's bold visual language to make his debut. Using a three-act structure, the film interleaves the film-within-the-film with reality: women beat violent partners with heavy objects, ruthless gangsters are punished by a mafia of organ resellers, and there is a choreographed musical number.

Reviewers read it as satire of the film industry and of the conflict between art and commerce; the Tallinn festival's programme called it an absurd Kyrgyz slapstick comedy.
honors: 入选｜2026 Golden Rooster Film Screening · 此刻：国际新片展映
gr26-068.editorial: At just 79 minutes, an orderly mess of black comedy for viewers curious about another face of Central Asian cinema. Some sequences are exaggerated; take them as parody of the industry.
gr26-068.contentNote: Available story information indicates: Social or professional pressure. Detailed depiction and intensity have not been verified; consider your individual needs.

gr26-069.title: Congo Boy
gr26-069.syn: A Congolese refugee teenager cares for four younger siblings in the Central African Republic while dreaming of becoming a musician.
gr26-069.bio: Rafiki Fariala was born in 1997 in Uvira, Democratic Republic of the Congo, and grew up as a Congolese refugee in Bangui, capital of the Central African Republic. In 2017 he joined an Ateliers Varan documentary workshop in Bangui and made the short Mbi Na Mo the following year; his documentary We, Students! played in the Berlinale Forum. Congo Boy is his first fiction feature, co-written with Tommy Baron and Boris Lojkine, with music and songs by Fariala himself. It played in Un Certain Regard at Cannes, where its lead Bradley Fiomona Dembeasset won Best Actor.
highlights: Best Actor in Un Certain Regard for first-time actor Bradley Fiomona Dembeasset.
The director grew up a Congolese refugee in Bangui; the film draws heavily on his own experience.
Shot entirely on location in Bangui, at night and handheld; songs and poetry are part of the storytelling.
Dialogue mixes Lingala, Sango, Swahili and French.
gr26-069.st:
The film had its world premiere in Un Certain Regard at Cannes on 15 May 2026. Seventeen-year-old Congolese refugee Robert is hanging on in Bangui through odd jobs and a little music; after his parents are jailed he must support his younger siblings alone, yet will not give up his dream of performing. The director grew up as a Congolese refugee in Bangui himself, and has said much of the film is drawn from his own experience, told through fiction in the character of Robert. Dialogue mixes Lingala, Sango, Swahili and French.

It was shot entirely on location in Bangui, much of it at night; Adrien Lallau's handheld, mobile camerawork immerses us in backstreet and nightclub life. Lead Bradley Fiomona Dembeasset acts for the first time; the songs he performs were written by Fariala with Lillo Morreale. Co-writer and producer Boris Lojkine directed Souleymane's Story.

Reviews praise its warmth: Screen Daily calls it warm, likeable and human; Variety notes a distinctive rhythm but uneven writing; Cineuropa finds it one of the more predictable titles at this year's Cannes.
gr26-069.editorial: Reviews generally say it avoids the usual rise-to-fame formula and uses songs and poems to get through the days. Watch Robert reciting verse on the streets and performing in clubs: they are both his dream and his way of surviving in Bangui.
gr26-069.contentNote: Available story information indicates: Refugee experiences; Confinement or displacement; Distress or pressure affecting children. Detailed depiction and intensity have not been verified; consider your individual needs.

gr26-070.title: The Innocent
gr26-070.syn: An aristocrat indulges his own affairs but cannot accept his wife's independence, turning jealousy into tragedy.
gr26-070.bio: Luchino Visconti was an Italian director whose work runs from neorealism to lavish period films. The Innocent was his last film; he directed it from a wheelchair after strokes and a broken leg, and was felled by a second stroke in March 1976 while it was in post-production, dying soon after. It was released posthumously.
highlights: Visconti's last film, made from a wheelchair and released after his death.
Adapted from D'Annunzio's 1892 novel.
Opened San Sebastián in competition in 1976; shown in Cannes Classics in 2026.
Photography by Pasqualino De Santis, costumes by Piero Tosi.
gr26-070.st:
The film adapts Gabriele D'Annunzio's 1892 novel L'innocente (often translated as The Intruder), written by Suso Cecchi d'Amico, Enrico Medioli and Visconti. Tullio, a Roman aristocrat (Giancarlo Giannini), openly sees his mistress Teresa (Jennifer O'Neill) but cannot accept his wife Giuliana's (Laura Antonelli) relationship with a writer; jealousy and possessiveness push the marriage toward tragedy.

According to the Cannes festival, Visconti first dreamed of Alain Delon, Romy Schneider and Helmut Berger, but ended up with Giannini, Antonelli and O'Neill. The film opens with the director's own aged hand turning the pages of the novel. Photography is by Pasqualino De Santis, production design by Mario Garbuglia and costumes by Piero Tosi.

It opened the San Sebastián festival in competition in 1976 and returned to Cannes in 2026 in Cannes Classics. Critic Andrew Sarris wrote that Visconti seems to savour the things of this world for the last time, and that no earlier Visconti film conveys such a sense of loss.
gr26-070.editorial: A slow, lavish psychological drama with meticulous settings, light and costumes, for patient viewers. It involves infidelity and harm to an infant, so check the content notes.
gr26-070.contentNote: Available story information indicates: Relationship conflict or coercion; Harm or death involving children; Death and bereavement. Detailed depiction and intensity have not been verified; consider your individual needs.

gr26-071.title: You Don’t Belong Here
gr26-071.syn: A widowed hospital director must confront his family's blind spots when his son becomes a suspect in a murder investigation.
gr26-071.bio: Florin Șerban was born on 21 January 1975 in Reșița, Romania. His debut feature If I Want to Whistle, I Whistle (2010) won the Silver Bear Grand Jury Prize in Berlin; he later made Box (2015). You Don't Belong Here is his return to the international stage after several years; it won the Golden Leopard in the 2026 Locarno competition, and he is writer, director and producer.
highlights: Golden Leopard at Locarno; Șerban's return to the international stage after several years, set in his home town of Reșița.
A xenophobic attack on a Roma man draws out patriarchy and violence between a hospital chief, his son and a police-inspector friend.
Romanian New Wave static long takes and restraint; praised as rigorous and powerful, but some find it cold and slow.
Underneath, a more basic question: do any of us really belong here?
gr26-071.st:
You Don't Belong Here (Romanian title Nu e locul tău aici) had its world premiere on 9 August 2026 in the International Competition of the 79th Locarno Film Festival, where it won the Golden Leopard. It is set in Șerban's home town of Reșița. In a cold night, a group of hooded cyclists slash tyres and paste stickers on cars; a Roma man comes out to challenge them and is beaten to the ground, and later dies, with his son asking the hospital not to perform an autopsy. The relationships between Marius (Adrian Văncică), chief of the small-town hospital, his son (Teodor Butănescu) and his police-inspector friend Silviu are gradually torn open.

Critics generally see the film using the New Wave toolkit of static long takes and restraint to address xenophobic violence, patriarchy, police corruption and violence across generations. Cineuropa calls it formally precise and powerful; Sight & Sound compares its patient elegance to Nuri Bilge Ceylan while finding it hard to connect with its clinical world; others fault its slow pace and a careless ending.
gr26-071.editorial: Long and coolly paced, for viewers willing to be patient with long takes and interested in Romanian society and patriarchy. Don't rush to decide who is right; notice how the camera keeps its distance from the characters throughout.
gr26-071.contentNote: Available story information indicates: Crime, threat or interpersonal conflict; Violence or injury; Death and bereavement. Detailed depiction and intensity have not been verified; consider your individual needs.

gr26-072.title: Gone with the Wind
gr26-072.syn: Scarlett O'Hara struggles through war, poverty and lost love as the old American South collapses around her.
gr26-072.bio: Victor Fleming was a Hollywood director who in 1939 completed both The Wizard of Oz and Gone with the Wind, the latter winning him the Oscar for Best Director. Gone with the Wind actually went through three directors: the original director George Cukor was dismissed, Fleming took over, and when he left briefly from exhaustion Sam Wood filled in; only Fleming is credited on screen.
highlights: Eight competitive Oscars plus two honorary awards; Hattie McDaniel was the first African American Oscar winner.
Three directors and more than a dozen writers; Selznick delayed production two years for Gable.
Premiered in Atlanta on 15 December 1939; 238 minutes including overture and intermission.
Its romanticised view of slavery and the South has long drawn criticism.
gr26-072.st:
The film adapts Margaret Mitchell's 1936 novel, produced by David O. Selznick with a screenplay by Sidney Howard and contributions from more than a dozen other writers. Selznick delayed the start of shooting by two years to secure Clark Gable as Rhett, with cameras rolling only in January 1939; Scarlett was cast after filming began. The production was turbulent, Selznick obsessed over every detail and the film went through three directors.

It premiered in Atlanta on 15 December 1939, cost about $4 million and set box-office records. At the 12th Academy Awards it received 13 nominations and won eight competitive Oscars (Picture, Director, Actress, Supporting Actress, Screenplay, Color Cinematography, Interior Decoration and Film Editing) plus two honorary awards. Hattie McDaniel became the first African American to win an Oscar, but segregation laws kept her from the Atlanta premiere.

Its romanticised view of slavery and the South has long been controversial, and it remains one of the most discussed films in cinema history.
gr26-072.editorial: The archetypal classical Hollywood epic, and one to watch with historical context: admire its scale and performances while noticing its angle on the South and slavery. It is very long and includes an intermission.
warnings: War, conflict or threat of war
gr26-072.contentNote: Also informed by a published overseas content advisory. The running time and cut may differ from this screening; consider your individual needs.

gr26-073.title: Princess Iron Fan
gr26-073.syn: Blocked by the Flaming Mountains, Monkey must obtain Princess Iron Fan's magical fan and overcome the Bull Demon King.
gr26-073.bio: Wan Laiming and Wan Guchan, two of the Wan brothers, are regarded as the founders of Chinese animation. In 1926 they made China's first animated short, Uproar in the Studio, in Shanghai, and in 1941 they made Princess Iron Fan, China's and Asia's first animated feature. Wan Laiming later directed Havoc in Heaven and first created Sun Wukong's animated image.
highlights: China's and Asia's first animated feature, released in 1941 in Shanghai's 'isolated island'.
Based on the episode of borrowing the plantain fan, with the Bull Demon King as a metaphor for the invaders.
A year and four months, over 100 people and nearly 20,000 drawings.
Said to have led Osamu Tezuka into animation.
gr26-073.st:
Disney's Snow White, shown in Nanjing and Shanghai in 1938, made the Wan brothers want a Chinese-style feature: if there could be a Snow White there could also be an Iron Fan Princess; another motive was to use the Bull Demon King as a metaphor for the Japanese invaders and lift wartime morale. They first wanted to make Havoc in Heaven but the company backed out for financial reasons; New China United Film (later merged into China United Film) then chose the Journey to the West episode of borrowing the plantain fan, and Zhang Shankun set a tight schedule before patriotic businessman Sheng Pihua funded it and stopped interfering.

Preparation began in June 1939, over 70 people were recruited in March 1940, and the work took a year and four months with more than 100 people, nearly 20,000 drawings and close to 20,000 feet of rushes; it was China's first sound animated feature, about 80 minutes long. It opened in 'isolated island' Shanghai in September 1941 and caused a sensation, then travelled to Southeast Asia and Japan. Osamu Tezuka, the 'father of Japanese anime', is said to have been so moved by it that he fell in love with animation; meeting Wan Laiming in Shanghai in 1981, he told him he had gone into animation after seeing his film.

It is also where Wan Laiming first created Sun Wukong's animated image, laying the ground for the later Havoc in Heaven.
honors: 入选｜2026 Golden Rooster Film Screening · 流光：动画展映单元
gr26-073.editorial: Black-and-white animation of historical value and childlike charm; note the early designs of Sun Wukong and Pigsy and how they resemble and differ from Disney.
gr26-073.contentNote: Available story information indicates: Violence or injury; Crime, threat or interpersonal conflict. Detailed depiction and intensity have not been verified; consider your individual needs.

gr26-074.title: Tender Loving Care
gr26-074.syn: A social worker moves in with a friend after a breakup, seeking mutual support while facing family illness and exhausting work.
gr26-074.bio: Mike Leigh, born in 1943, is a British director and writer known for developing his films through long rehearsal and improvisation with his actors. His credits include Secrets & Lies (Palme d'Or, Cannes 1996), Vera Drake (Golden Lion, Venice 2004), Mr. Turner, Peterloo and Hard Truths (2024). Tender Loving Care won the Golden Shell for Best Film in competition at San Sebastián in September 2026; the press reports that it may be his last feature.
highlights: Golden Shell for Best Film and Best Screenplay at San Sebastián; Kate O'Flynn shared the Silver Shell for Best Leading Performance.
Four equally weighted performances: Amy and her friend Rosie, and Amy's ageing parents.
Friendship, everyday care, ageing and the toll of social work; also read as a critique of the British welfare system.
Leigh's customary long rehearsal and improvisation; the press says it may be his last feature.
gr26-074.st:
The film had its world premiere at Telluride in September 2026, then screened in Toronto, before competing at the 74th San Sebastián festival. There it won the Golden Shell for Best Film and Best Screenplay; Kate O'Flynn took the Silver Shell for Best Leading Performance (shared with Asta Kamma August for Growth of the Soil), and the film also won the Transforma Make & Mark Award.

It centres on four people: Amy (Kate O'Flynn) and her friend Rosie (Alice Bailey Johnson), and Amy's ageing parents Birdie (Marion Bailey) and Fred (Paul Jesson). Accepting her prize, O'Flynn described an equally weighted quartet and dedicated the award to her three co-stars. The film is about friendship, everyday care, ageing and the toll of heavy work.

Reviews generally find it plainer than his recent Mr. Turner, Peterloo and Hard Truths; DMovies calls it both a swipe at the British welfare system and a love letter to old age.
gr26-074.editorial: If you like Leigh looking at people through small everyday things, this is plainer than his recent films: unhurried, resting on dialogue and expression. Notice the ease between the four actors, as if they had lived together for years, and how homely lines hide pressure.
gr26-074.contentNote: Available story information indicates: Relationship conflict or coercion; Illness, treatment or care; Ageing and care. Detailed depiction and intensity have not been verified; consider your individual needs.

gr26-075.title: Chronicles from the Siege
gr26-075.syn: Under siege, ordinary residents struggle to preserve love, friendship and everyday life amid hunger, violence and isolation.
gr26-075.bio: Abdallah Al-Khatib was born in Damascus in 1989 and is a Palestinian-Syrian director, writer and researcher based in Germany. His first feature documentary, Little Palestine: Diary of a Siege (2021), about life in the besieged Yarmouk refugee camp, won the Interreligious Award at Visions du Réel, among others. Chronicles from the Siege is his first fiction feature; it premiered in the Perspectives section of the 76th Berlinale in 2026 and won the GWFF Best First Feature Award.
highlights: GWFF Best First Feature Award in the Berlinale's Perspectives section; the director's first fiction feature.
The city is never named but resembles Gaza; drawn from the Yarmouk siege and stories gathered from Gaza.
A cigarette, the last scraps of food, a tryst between bombardments: survival told through small scenes.
Dark humour alongside grief; the director appears as a cigarette thief.
gr26-075.st:
The film had its world premiere in the Perspectives section of the Berlinale on 15 February 2026. It is made of interwoven vignettes set in a besieged city that is never named but resembles Gaza. Critics note that it draws partly on the director's own experience of the siege of Yarmouk and partly on stories gathered from Gaza in recent years; Al-Khatib also appears briefly as a cigarette thief.

Its episodes are small and concrete: a group desperate for a single puff, a starving old man scraping together what food remains in his home, lovers trying to complete a tryst between bombardments. Film Comment calls it angry yet compassionate; Variety finds it harrowing, poignant and at times darkly hilarious.

It was produced by Algeria's Issaad Film (producer Taqiyeddine Issaad) and Evidence Film, supported by the Doha Film Institute, with sales by Paris-based Loco Films. It won the GWFF Best First Feature Award in Berlin and has since played festivals including Melbourne.
gr26-075.editorial: Heavy content: bombardment, hunger and death, though not only grief. Notice where the laughs come from and how each small story turns the siege from a place into a condition of living.
warnings: War, conflict or threat of war
gr26-075.contentNote: Available story information indicates: War, conflict or threat of war; Death and bereavement. Detailed depiction and intensity have not been verified; consider your individual needs.

gr26-076.title: All About Corinne
gr26-076.syn: A longtime extra befriends a famous actress, hoping for a breakthrough while confronting the barriers behind cinema's glamorous surface.
gr26-076.bio: Marc Fitoussi, born on 20 July 1976, is a French director and screenwriter. His first feature La Vie d'artiste won the Prix Michel d'Ornano at the Deauville American Film Festival; Copacabana (2010) starred Isabelle Huppert with her daughter Lolita Chammah, and he followed with Folies Bergère (2014), Selfie (2020) and Two Tickets to Greece (2022). All About Corinne (Ni vue, ni connue) premiered in Locarno's Piazza Grande in 2026.
highlights: Premiered in Locarno's Piazza Grande, shown in TIFF's Gala section, and opened the El Gouna festival.
Huppert plays a background actor who never gets her chance: one of cinema's most familiar faces as an invisible player.
Kiberlain, Bercot, Kruger and others appear as themselves in a self-mocking satire of the film world.
The English title nods to All About Eve.
gr26-076.st:
The film premiered in Locarno's Piazza Grande on 15 August 2026, then played TIFF's Gala section and Busan, and opened the El Gouna festival; Cohen Media Group handles North America. Corinne Maclou (Isabelle Huppert) has long been a background actor; she hands out her CV, roams sets, and cosies up to famous actress Sandrine Kiberlain in the hope of finally being seen. Kiberlain plays herself, an imperious and insecure star.

Several French film figures appear as themselves: Emmanuelle Bercot is a director shooting a big-budget period drama, and Diane Kruger is, in Variety's words, hilariously glamazonian. The English title nods to the Hollywood classic All About Eve. The director says that using Huppert, among the most familiar of faces, to play an invisible actress is the film's challenge and its amusing paradox.

Reviews differ: Deadline and Variety find it witty and delightful, while DMovies finds it contrived and disconnected from reality.
honors: 入选｜2026 Golden Rooster Film Screening · 此刻：国际新片展映
gr26-076.editorial: If you enjoy inside jokes about French cinema it will be funnier, but it works without them: the core is the wish to be seen. Notice how the film places a star like Huppert in a position of perpetual neglect.
gr26-076.contentNote: Available story information indicates: Social inequality or workplace mistreatment; Social or professional pressure. Detailed depiction and intensity have not been verified; consider your individual needs.

gr26-077.title: Inception
gr26-077.syn: A specialist in entering dreams attempts to plant an idea in a target's subconscious while confronting his own guilt and memories.
gr26-077.bio: Christopher Nolan was born in London on 30 July 1970 to an American mother and a British father. His company Syncopy, run with wife Emma Thomas, produced Inception; he went on to make Interstellar, Dunkirk, Tenet and Oppenheimer, shooting several films on IMAX and 70mm film.
highlights: About ten years in the making; first conceived as a horror film.
Eight Oscar nominations and four wins: Cinematography, Sound Editing, Sound Mixing and Visual Effects.
Different colour palettes mark dream layers, with many practical sets.
Hans Zimmer's score, with its signature low brass blast.
gr26-077.st:
Nolan has said the story took about ten years to crack: according to the Los Angeles Times he had the idea at sixteen and wrote a first draft around 2002, originally as a horror film, and began working on it in earnest only after The Dark Knight. Many ideas about Cobb came from Leonardo DiCaprio. The budget was about $160 million and the working title was Oliver's Arrow.

Cinematographer Wally Pfister used different colour palettes for each dream layer; he and Nolan considered a 3D conversion but dropped it because of the story's complexity. Hans Zimmer's score is about sixty percent electronic, and its low brass blast became the film's signature. It premiered in London on 8 July 2010, opened on 16 July and grossed over $800 million worldwide.

Inception received eight Oscar nominations (including Best Picture and Original Screenplay) and won four: Cinematography, Sound Editing, Sound Mixing and Visual Effects.
gr26-077.editorial: The layered dream structure takes concentration, but the emotional line is simple: a man weighed by guilt wants to go home. The ending's spinning top need not have an answer; you can leave the cinema with the question.
gr26-077.contentNote: Available story information indicates: Violence or injury; Death and bereavement; Psychological distress or uncertainty. Detailed depiction and intensity have not been verified; consider your individual needs.

gr26-078.title: Ground Floor
gr26-078.syn: A man investigates mould in his apartment and becomes trapped in a building-wide tangle of evasion, secrecy and competing interests.
gr26-078.bio: Gábor Reisz was born in Budapest on 19 January 1980 and studied film theory and history at Eötvös Loránd University. His Explanation for Everything (2023) won the Orizzonti prize for Best Film in Venice, and he returned as a jury member the following year. Ground Floor (Földszint) is his fourth feature, premiering in the Venice Spotlight section in 2026, co-written with Éva Schulze as a Hungarian-Italian co-production.
highlights: World premiere in Venice Spotlight; the director's previous film Explanation for Everything won the Orizzonti prize for Best Film.
A patch of black mould unravels a whole building's evasions, snitching and vested interests.
A grotesque comedy; critics read the apartment block as a metaphor for Hungarian society.
He learns he will be a father on the day he finds the mould: private life and social pressure arrive together.
gr26-078.st:
The film had its world premiere in the Venice Spotlight section of the 83rd Venice Film Festival in 2026. Its hero Kristóf (Ádám Tompa) is a former painter now working as a bank archivist; on the same day he learns he will become a father he discovers black mould spreading on the wall of his ground-floor flat. He sets out to trace where the water comes from and moves through the whole building: snitching superintendents, corrupt building managers, a drunken mould specialist. A small repair becomes a Kafkaesque journey.

Venice artistic director Alberto Barbera describes it as a grotesque comedy that can be read as a coded allegory of the previous regime; Cineuropa calls the mould a clear metaphor for Orbán-era Hungary. It is produced by Proton Cinema (Juli Berkes) with Italian producer Andrea Romeo.

His previous film, Explanation for Everything, won the Orizzonti prize in 2023 and likewise placed an individual's predicament inside a larger social mood.
gr26-078.editorial: Suited to viewers who like absurdist comedy with some social satire. Notice how neighbours on each floor dodge the same problem in different ways, and how Kristóf, who only wants the wall fixed, is gradually pulled in.
gr26-078.contentNote: Available story information indicates: Unsafe housing; Sexual or reproductive themes; Neighbour conflict. Detailed depiction and intensity have not been verified; consider your individual needs.

gr26-079.title: Visitation
gr26-079.syn: A lakeside house near Berlin witnesses successive residents, persecution, exile, division and reunification over a turbulent century.
gr26-079.bio: Volker Schlöndorff was born in Wiesbaden on 31 March 1939 and is a leading figure of New German Cinema. His first feature, Young Törless (1966), won the FIPRESCI Prize at Cannes, and The Tin Drum (1979) won the Palme d'Or. Visitation is his 28th film, shown in Cannes Première in 2026 when he was 87.
highlights: Schlöndorff's 28th film, shown in Cannes Première.
One lakeside house witnesses the Nazi era, war and exile, division and reunification.
Shot in Einstein's holiday home, with the crew working there for a full year.
Adapted from Jenny Erpenbeck's novel, with Martina Gedeck, Lars Eidinger and Susanne Wolff.
gr26-079.st:
The film is adapted from Jenny Erpenbeck's novel Heimsuchung (English edition 2010); Schlöndorff wrote the script himself and calls it a free adaptation. It centres on a house by a lake near Berlin where several families live in turn: from the Nazi era, war and exile, through the division of Germany to the fall of the Berlin Wall, the house barely changes while its people keep losing, searching and redefining what home means.

In Cannes' official interview the director says the house is not a set but Albert Einstein's holiday home, which he had to flee when the Nazis came to power; a young Bauhaus architect had designed it. The house was in fact some 40 kilometres from the lake, so the film puts it beside the water. The crew could come and go for a whole year, and the actors and children grew accustomed to it.

The cast includes Martina Gedeck, Lars Eidinger, Susanne Wolff and Ulrich Matthes, with cinematography by Axel Schneppat. Cineuropa calls it meticulously crafted and tenderly intimate, a historical epic spanning nearly a century; RogerEbert.com feels the wide scope makes some events plod while others lose clarity. It opened in Germany on 15 October 2026.
gr26-079.editorial: The film spans a long time with many characters, so watch the house itself first: how its walls, windows and lake are passed to new owners across the decades. If you like literary adaptations or modern German history, it is easier to enter.
warnings: War, conflict or threat of war
gr26-079.contentNote: Available story information indicates: Nazi-era persecution and its aftermath; War, conflict or threat of war; Migration or displacement. Detailed depiction and intensity have not been verified; consider your individual needs.

gr26-080.title: Viva Carmen!
gr26-080.syn: Street children in Seville try to save the spirited Carmen from a tragic fate foretold by a prophecy.
gr26-080.bio: Sébastien Laudenbach is a French animation director. The Girl Without Hands (2016) was his first animated feature; Chicken for Linda!, co-directed with Chiara Malta (2023), won the Cristal at Annecy and the César for Best Animated Film. Viva Carmen is his third animated feature; it premiered in Directors' Fortnight at Cannes in 2026, then competed at Annecy and played the Centrepiece section at TIFF.
highlights: Premiered in Directors' Fortnight, then competed at Annecy and played the Centrepiece section at TIFF.
Retells Carmen through the street children of the opera's opening chorus.
Vividly coloured, like a handmade storybook; most of the opera's music is replaced by a new score.
Music by Amine Bouhafa and flamenco guitarist Isabelle Laudenbach.
gr26-080.st:
The film is adapted from Bizet's opera Carmen (itself based on Mérimée's novella), from an original idea by producer Pierre-Henri Léon and the director, with a screenplay by Santiago Otheguy and Laudenbach. It is set in Seville in 1820: Salvador, young assistant to the knife grinder Antonio, meets the captivating, free-spirited Carmen. Antonio can glimpse the future in sharpened blades and foresees that she will die at the hands of the soldier José. Salvador and a band of street kids led by Belén decide to defy fate and save her. Laudenbach takes the children's chorus that opens the opera as his entry point and retells the story through the street kids' eyes.

He told Variety in Cannes that he wanted to show a real woman rather than an icon: her priority is not love but freedom, and she is willing to pay the ultimate price for it. The film trims most of the opera's music, with a new score by Amine Bouhafa and the director's sister, flamenco guitarist Isabelle Laudenbach; Variety says the visuals do the singing.

Produced by Folivari, it was later completed in a Spanish-language version with a new song by singer Silvia Pérez Cruz, and opens in France on 16 December 2026.
gr26-080.editorial: No need to know the opera: it enters through the children, and Carmen is a woman who values freedom above love. Come for the hand-drawn animation and colour.
gr26-080.contentNote: Available story information indicates: Crime, threat or interpersonal conflict; Death and bereavement. Detailed depiction and intensity have not been verified; consider your individual needs.

gr26-081.title: Princess Peacock
gr26-081.syn: A prince seeks his beloved peacock princess after court intrigue forces them apart, facing trials of courage and loyalty.
gr26-081.bio: Jin Xi, from Tianjin, began studying painting in 1936, joined the Eighth Route Army when the war broke out, and after 1949 became one of the first directors to make puppet animation. His 1955 The Magic Brush was the first Chinese animation to win awards abroad, bringing back five; the 1963 The Peacock Princess is China's first colour puppet feature.
highlights: China's first colour puppet feature, adapted from the Dai epic poem Zhao Shutun.
Characters designed by painter Cheng Shifa.
Jin Xi's 1955 The Magic Brush was the first Chinese animation to win abroad.
Uses Dai costumes, architecture and dance.
gr26-081.st:
Written by Jin Xi and Yin Kouyang and directed by Jin Xi, the film was produced by the Shanghai Animation Film Studio in 1963 and adapts the Dai epic poem Zhao Shutun, with character designs by painter Cheng Shifa. Puppet animation was the direction Jin explored throughout the early People's Republic: in 1953 he made the first colour puppet film The Little Hero and afterwards reflected that it was influenced by Western Europe and lacked national style; in 1954 he visited Czech puppet master Jiří Trnka at the Karlovy Vary festival and toured his studio, then made The Magic Brush, seen as the beginning of a national style.

The Peacock Princess tells of Prince Zhao Shutun who falls in love with the Peacock Princess, but a treacherous minister's slander forces her to leave and the prince goes through hardships to follow her; running time varies by source (about 73 to 80 minutes). It uses Dai costumes, architecture and dance, an attempt at a feature-length Chinese puppet film.
honors: 入选｜2026 Golden Rooster Film Screening · 流光：动画展映单元
gr26-081.editorial: A puppet film good for children and a record of the craft of Shanghai's animation studio in the 1960s; note the handling of Dai costume and dance.
gr26-081.contentNote: Available story information indicates: Confinement or displacement; Relationship conflict or coercion; Dangerous situations or accidents. Detailed depiction and intensity have not been verified; consider your individual needs.

gr26-082.title: Prince Nezha’s Triumph Against Dragon King
gr26-082.syn: Young Nezha defies the Dragon King to protect his people, sacrificing himself before returning through a miraculous rebirth.
gr26-082.bio: Nezha Conquers the Dragon King was co-directed by Wang Shuchen, Yan Dingxian and Xu Jingda (Ada), with overall art design by painter Zhang Ding, then head of the Central Academy of Arts and Design. Made by the Shanghai Animation Film Studio for the 30th anniversary of the People's Republic in 1979, it is China's first widescreen animated feature.
highlights: China's first widescreen animated feature, made by the Shanghai studio for the 30th anniversary of the PRC.
Painter Zhang Ding as art designer, drawing on Dunhuang and Yongle Palace murals.
Co-directed by three directors over 15 months.
Won the Hundred Flowers award for best art film and showed at Cannes.
gr26-082.st:
A first draft of the script was finished in the late 1950s, when a co-production with the Moscow animation studio was planned; the partnership stopped and the script sat for twenty years. In 1977 the Shanghai studio sought a subject that could carry on national culture while breaking new ground, director Wang Shuchen dug out the script, and it became the key film for the 30th anniversary of the founding of the People's Republic, with what was described as the strongest directing team ever. Production began in May 1978 and took 15 months, a hand-drawn tour de force.

Zhang Ding was invited in the summer of 1978 as chief art designer and went from field research to character design in two months; drawing on Dunhuang and Yongle Palace murals and folk New Year prints and woodcuts, he combined decorative lines with the folk palette of cyan, green, red, white and black to achieve an aesthetic that is both familiar and fresh. The story comes from Investiture of the Gods, but the filmmakers did not copy it: Nezha became a lively, endearing youth unafraid of power, and Li Jing a father with tenderness toward his child; Nezha's suicide scene remains vivid for many viewers.

It was released on 19 May 1979, won the Best Art Film prize at the third Hundred Flowers Awards in 1980 and was shown at Cannes; director Jiaozi has said the 1979 version was the starting point of his new Ne Zha.
gr26-082.dir: Wang Shuchen / Yan Dingxian / A Da
gr26-082.editorial: If you have just seen the new Ne Zha, go back to the 1979 source: decorative imagery, Peking-opera rhythm and a youthful hero's tragedy. Nezha's suicide scene is heavy, so take care with young children.
gr26-082.contentNote: Available story information indicates: Harm or death involving children; Self-harm and self-sacrifice; Violence or injury. Detailed depiction and intensity have not been verified; consider your individual needs.
gr26-082.dirLife: Wang Shuchen · Yan Dingxian · Xu Jingda (Ada) · China

gr26-083.title: Chinese Animation: A Century
gr26-083.syn: Archival footage and artists' recollections trace a century of Chinese animation and the development of its distinctive artistic traditions.
gr26-083.bio: Sun Lijun, former vice president of the Beijing Film Academy and head of the China Animation Research Institute, is chief director of Chinese Animation: A Century, with credits including Little Soldier Zhang Ga and Legend of a Rabbit. Feng Yabing is director and writer, and Yang Zhifeng co-director and editing consultant.
highlights: Reviews a century of Chinese animation, 1922–2022, drawing on more than fifty works.
Interviews over a hundred animators and collects much unreleased material.
Outstanding Film Award at Russia's Northern People International Film Festival in 2024.
Combines live shooting with hand-drawn restoration to reproduce lost techniques.
gr26-083.st:
In December 2022 a seminar titled 'A Century of Chinese Animation: Review, Reflection and Outlook' and the documentary's launch were held; Sun Lijun proposed and led the China Animation Research Institute of the Beijing Film Academy together with the Shanghai Animation Film Studio to launch a series of 'Century of Chinese Animation' activities, of which the film is part. It is a National Publishing Fund project produced by the Ministry of Education's educational technology resource centre with the Shanghai studio.

According to reports, the team prepared for years, consulted millions of words of documents and archives, travelled to more than ten cities and visited the Shanghai Animation Film Studio and other old creative bases, interviewing over a hundred veteran animation artists, industry leaders, scholars and newcomers and collecting many unreleased films, manuscripts, working photos and oral records; it combines traditional live shooting with hand-drawn restoration, reproducing some lost traditional animation techniques. It features more than fifty works including Havoc in Heaven, Where Is Mama, The Legend of Sealed Book, Nezha Conquers the Dragon King, Monkey King: Hero Is Back and Ne Zha.

It opened the Guangdong–Hong Kong–Macao Greater Bay Area Animation Film Week in October 2024, was selected in November that year for Russia's Northern People International Film Festival, winning the outstanding film award with a special contribution award for Sun Lijun, and opened in Chinese cinemas on 1 June 2026.
honors: 入选｜2026 Golden Rooster Film Screening · 流光：动画展映单元
gr26-083.editorial: A primer on the Chinese school of animation: see Princess Iron Fan and Nezha Conquers the Dragon King first and it will resonate more. It is a documentary built on archives and interviews.
gr26-083.contentNote: The available synopsis has been reviewed, but no specific sensitive content has been established. This is not an all-ages assurance or a full content assessment.

amrum.title: Amrum
amrum.syn: A historical drama set in spring 1945, in the last days of the Second World War, centred on ten-year-old Nanning. With his father away at the front, the boy does everything he can to help his mother feed the family: hunting seals, fishing at night, working the fields. But the long-awaited peace brings new conflict, and Nanning must find his own course among the ruins.
honors: 提名｜2026 ASC Awards · Spotlight Award
获奖｜2026 Bavarian Film Awards · Best Film
提名｜2026 German Film Awards · Outstanding Feature Film / Best Cinematography / Best Sound / Best Film Score / Best Costume Design / Best Makeup
highlights: The story comes from Hark Bohm's own childhood; Akin took it on as a way of fulfilling a friend's wish, so the film carries both personal memory and a handing-down between directors.
It is Akin's first film about Germany's own wartime history, seen through the eyes of a ten-year-old as the loss of paradise.
Much of the film is about a child finding food for his family: hunting seals, fishing at night, working the fields. Hunger gives the war its most concrete shape.
Shot by Independence Day cinematographer Lindenlaub, the sea, wind and fields of a North Sea island are the stars of the image; the film was nominated for the ASC Spotlight Award.
amrum.bio: Fatih Akin was born in Hamburg in 1973 to a Turkish immigrant family and is one of the most internationally recognised European directors of his generation. He won the Golden Bear in Berlin in 2004 for Head-On (Gegen die Wand), the Special Jury Prize in Venice in 2009 for Soul Kitchen, and competed for the Palme d'Or at Cannes in 2017 with In the Fade (Aus dem Nichts), which he co-wrote with Hark Bohm. Amrum is his twelfth feature and the first in which he turns directly to Germany's own wartime history. As a teenager he was deeply influenced by Bohm's films such as Nordsee ist Mordsee and Moritz, lieber Moritz; the two were close friends and mentor and pupil for many years. Bohm died in November 2025 at the age of 86.
amrum.st:
Amrum is drawn from the childhood memories of director Hark Bohm. Bohm had meant to direct it himself; after telling Akin about his childhood, he was encouraged to make it into a film, and in the end he handed the direction to his long-time friend, who rewrote Bohm's original script and directed it. Akin calls the film very special and unusual for him: a journey into the depths of his 'German soul' and, perhaps, the last lesson Bohm taught him.

Shooting ran from 22 April to 25 June 2024 in Hamburg, on the island of Amrum and in Denmark. The cinematographer is Karl Walter Lindenlaub (Independence Day) and the editor Andrew Bird (The Seed of the Sacred Fig, Head-On); it was produced by Akin's Bombero International and Warner Bros. Film Productions Germany with Rialto Film. Twelve-year-old Jasper Billerbeck plays Nanning, Diane Kruger reunites with Akin, and Bohm himself appears as the old man by the sea.

The film had its world premiere on 15 May 2025 in the Cannes Premiere section of the 78th Cannes Film Festival and later won Best Film at the 2026 Bavarian Film Awards. Akin describes the story as an expulsion from paradise: in the last weeks of the war the children are not sent to the front, yet they carry responsibility for their families' food and future.
amrum.editorial: Suited to viewers who like historical drama and coming-of-age stories. Watch the disagreement between the boy and his mother: the end of the war does not mean old ideas at home disappear with it. It also rewards comparison with Akin's earlier work on migration and identity, and how he handles the idea of being German here.
amrum.contentNote: Available story information indicates: Nazi-era persecution and its aftermath; Animal harm or death themes; Family conflict or separation. Detailed depiction and intensity have not been verified; consider your individual needs.

dry-leaf.title: Dry Leaf
dry-leaf.syn: Photographer Lisa suddenly disappears. The last clues point to seven football pitches she photographed, scattered across seven remote Georgian villages. Her father Irakli travels from pitch to pitch looking for her, and Lisa's ghost-like best friend Levani quietly joins the search. As the pitches change, villagers and their stories pass by like a carousel. Beneath the seemingly absurd journey, something darker builds: with every pitted field and every silent village, the hope of finding Lisa thins like morning mist.
honors: 提名｜2025 Locarno Film Festival · Golden Leopard, Best Film
获奖｜2025 Locarno Film Festival · Golden Leopard, Special Mention
获奖｜2025 Locarno Film Festival · FIPRESCI Prize
提名｜2025 Entrevues Belfort Film Festival · Grand Prix Janine Bazin
提名｜2025 Hainan Island International Film Festival · Golden Coconut, Best Picture
获奖｜2025 Bangkok International Film Festival · Grand Prix
获奖｜2025 Pančevo International Film Festival · Best Film
highlights: A road movie about searching for a missing daughter that spends most of its time on football pitches, villages and chance encounters.
Shot entirely on an old mobile phone, its rough low-resolution image carries nostalgia and makes people and land hard to tell apart.
Written, shot and edited by the director alone, with music and sound by his brother and his father in the lead: a near-family-workshop way of making a film.
Festival notes call it a whimsical love letter to his homeland, to football, and to art made from nothing.
dry-leaf.bio: Alexandre Koberidze was born in Tbilisi, Georgia, studied directing at the German Film and Television Academy Berlin (DFFB) and lives in Berlin. His early shorts include Der Fall (2014), Colophon (2015) and The Perfect Spectator (2017); his first feature Let the Summer Never Come Again (2017) won the top prize at FIDMarseille, and his second, What Do We See When We Look at the Sky? (2021), premiered at the Berlinale and won the FIPRESCI Prize. Dry Leaf is his third feature: he is writer, cinematographer and editor, his brother Giorgi Koberidze composes the music and designs the sound, and his father David Koberidze plays the lead.
dry-leaf.st:
The title comes from the football term 'folha seca' (Portuguese for 'dry leaf'), a free kick whose landing is hard to predict. Nino and Irakli's daughter Lisa, a sports photographer, vanishes after leaving a letter asking not to be found. Her father cannot let go: he drives across rural Georgia, asking in every town the same question, 'Is there a football field around here?'

The whole film was shot on an old Sony Ericsson W595 mobile phone; the low-resolution image lets people and places merge. In interviews Koberidze talks about the sacrifices of older generations and how the phone sharpened his eye. It is a German-Georgian co-production by New Matter Films and runs 186 minutes.

It had its world premiere on 13 August 2025 in the International Competition of the 78th Locarno Film Festival, winning a Golden Leopard Special Mention and the FIPRESCI Prize, then the Grand Prix at the Bangkok International Film Festival and Best Film at Pančevo, and was named one of the top ten films of 2025 in Sight & Sound's poll.
dry-leaf.editorial: For viewers willing to slow down. Don't rush to ask where the daughter has gone; watch for the football pitch in each town, the small talk and the unforced humour. It runs 186 minutes, so allow plenty of time.
dry-leaf.contentNote: Available story information indicates: Missing loved ones; Emotional distress or trauma. Detailed depiction and intensity have not been verified; consider your individual needs.

i-understand-your-displeasure.title: I Understand Your Displeasure
i-understand-your-displeasure.syn: Heike (59) is a customer service manager at a cleaning company, coordinating between clients, management and the cleaning staff. Her company is in conflict with an important subcontractor because Heike broke the rules trying to poach an informal worker from his team. The subcontractor now threatens to withdraw his support unless she secures more hours and income for him. To satisfy him, Heike has to dismiss one of her own staff, a colleague her friend Taya values highly. Heike feels increasingly torn between her responsibility to her team and the realities of a low-wage industry.
honors: 获奖｜2026 Hong Kong International Film Festival · Young Cinema Competition (World), Best Actress
入围｜2026 Berlin International Film Festival · Panorama
获奖｜2026 First Steps Award · Best Feature Film
获奖｜2026 Kinofest Lünen · Acting Prize for Lead Actress (Sabine Thalau)
highlights: The director has worked in cleaning himself and says he never stops researching, because reality keeps changing; the script is built on that.
Lead actress Sabine Thalau, a non-professional from the cleaning industry, won the Golden Firebird for Best Actress at the Hong Kong International Film Festival.
Instead of accusing, the film follows Heike's series of reasonable-looking decisions and shows how pressure pushes a person into isolation.
A continuation of Nuclear Nomads: more attention to workers rarely seen on screen.
i-understand-your-displeasure.st:
The film takes on the cleaning industry, one of Germany's largest service sectors. The director says it began from personal experience, and from wanting to look at the isolation of a trade in which everyone cleans alone: low pay and a piece-rate rhythm push colleagues to compete instead of standing together. Heike, a team leader, is told that to meet a contract she must sacrifice one of her own employees. As the pressure closes in she revives her dream of founding her own cleaning company, only to find she has burned too many bridges with her colleagues.

The film is shot in a near-observational mode, without sermonising or spectacle. Lead actress Sabine Thalau comes from the cleaning trade and is a non-professional; Friedrich talks about the authenticity she brings. The script is by Friedrich with Tünde Sautier and Daniel Kunz, produced by WennDann Film, with Films Boutique handling world sales.

It premiered on 13 February 2026 in the Panorama section of the 76th Berlinale, then won the First Steps Award for Best Feature Film; Sabine Thalau won the Golden Firebird for Best Actress at the Hong Kong International Film Festival and the lead acting prize at Kinofest Lünen.
i-understand-your-displeasure.editorial: For viewers interested in labour, class and the workplace. Watch each small trade-off Heike makes with her colleagues: individually they make sense, together they reveal the pressure of the system. The pace is tight and the mood oppressive, so you may want some time to decompress afterwards.
i-understand-your-displeasure.contentNote: Available story information indicates: Social inequality or workplace mistreatment; Financial hardship or exploitation. Detailed depiction and intensity have not been verified; consider your individual needs.
i-understand-your-displeasure.bio: Kilian Armando Friedrich was born in Konstanz, Germany, in 1995 and grew up in a border region between France and Germany once shaped by coal and steel; the factories there closed during his childhood. He studied acting in Hildesheim and Madrid, then documentary directing in Munich and Mexico City. Between finishing school and starting university he worked for about eight months in the cleaning industry, the experience this film grew from. His documentary Nuclear Nomads (Nomades du nucléaire), co-directed with Tizian Stromp Zargari and about temporary workers who clean nuclear reactors, premiered at the Berlinale in 2023 and won the German Short Film Award in the medium-length category. I Understand Your Displeasure is his first fiction feature.

karla.title: Karla
karla.syn: Set in Munich in 1962, the film tells the true story of 12-year-old Karla, who files a complaint against her father, seeking protection from his years of abuse. As she navigates the legal system, she forms a special bond with Judge Lamy, who becomes her beacon of hope. Karla is reluctant to reveal the full extent of her suffering, which gradually forces Judge Lamy to give her the freedom to tell her story on her own terms, a choice that puts his own career at risk.
honors: 获奖｜2026 Bavarian Film Awards · Best Screenplay, Best Actor
获奖｜2025 Munich Film Festival · German Cinema New Talent Award, Best Director and Best Screenplay
提名｜2026 Göteborg Film Festival · Ingmar Bergman Award, Best Debut Feature
highlights: Based on a real 1962 case: a twelve-year-old walks into a police station and takes her father to court.
The film uses flashbacks with restraint and shows no violence, saving its strength for how a child comes to be heard.
Lead actress Elise Krieps appears in a film for the first time; the Luxembourg film festival called it an impressive breakout role.
Directed and written by women, it won the German Cinema New Talent Awards for Best Director and Best Screenplay at the Munich Film Festival.
karla.bio: Christina Tournatzés (also spelled Tournatzès) was born in 1992 to a German-Greek background, lives in Munich, and graduated in 2019 from Macromedia University of Applied Sciences in Munich, where she studied directing. Karla is her first feature, written by Yvonne Görlach and produced by achtung panda! in Munich, with international sales handled by The Playmaker Munich; it was shown to international buyers at the 2025 Cannes film market. The film reflects her interest in trauma wrapped in silence and in the position of children within institutions.
karla.st:
The film is based on a real 1962 case in Munich: after studying law in the library, twelve-year-old Karla walks into a police station and asks to see a judge, to bring charges against the father who has abused her for years. One review calls it a milestone German case, the first in which a child sought a legal response to an abusive parent. Through discreet flashbacks, director Christina Tournatzés and cinematographer Florian Emmerich only hint at what happened, keeping the focus on how she finds the words and who is willing to listen.

Judge Lamy (Rainer Bock) takes the case on reluctantly; Karla's refusal to disclose everything at once forces him to give her the freedom to tell her story on her own terms, at risk to his own career. The trust that gradually forms between them is the film's emotional axis. Lead actress Elise Krieps, daughter of Vicky Krieps, makes her screen debut; German actors such as Imogen Kogge (The Zone of Interest) and Rainer Bock (The White Ribbon) support her.

It premiered at the Munich Film Festival in June 2025, winning German Cinema New Talent Awards for Best Director and Best Screenplay, was nominated in the Ingmar Bergman Competition for debuts at the Gothenburg Film Festival, and won Best Screenplay and Best Lead Performance at the 2026 Bavarian Film Awards.
karla.editorial: For viewers concerned with children's rights, the law and social silence. Watch how the judge and Karla slowly build trust, and how the film shows what it means to be believed. The subject is child abuse; it is told with restraint but is emotionally heavy, so please choose according to your own circumstances.
warnings: Violence against women or domestic abuse
karla.contentNote: Available story information indicates: Child abuse; Violence against women or domestic abuse; Distressing legal proceedings. Detailed depiction and intensity have not been verified; consider your individual needs.

miroirs-no-3.title: Miroirs No. 3
miroirs-no-3.syn: On a weekend trip to the countryside, Laura miraculously survives a car crash. Physically unharmed but deeply shaken, she is taken in by Betty, a witness to the accident, who cares for her attentively. Gradually Betty's husband and son also accept Laura's presence, and a family-like calm returns to the house. But before long, the shadows of the past come back…
honors: 提名｜2025 Cannes Film Festival · Directors’ Fortnight
提名｜2025 Sydney Film Festival · Sydney Film Prize, Best Film
highlights: The title comes from Ravel's 'A Boat on the Ocean'; the music echoes a story of a drifting person taken in.
Petzold's fourth consecutive collaboration with Paula Beer, whose relationship is the core of his recent films.
He calls it a ghost story and another variation on Vertigo; mirrors and doubles recur as themes.
At only 86 minutes; Reverse Shot's review calls it a softer film than Petzold has ever made.
miroirs-no-3.bio: Christian Petzold was born in Hilden, Germany, in 1960 and is a leading figure of the Berlin School. He won the Silver Bear for Best Director in Berlin in 2012 for Barbara; his later films Phoenix (2014), Transit, Undine (2020) and Afire (2023) were all acclaimed internationally, and Afire won the Silver Bear Grand Jury Prize. He has long worked with actress Paula Beer; Miroirs No. 3 is their fourth consecutive collaboration, his eleventh feature, and his first selection at Cannes. He is also the new president of the Viennale, which opened its 2025 edition with this film.
miroirs-no-3.st:
The title comes from the third piece of Ravel's piano suite Miroirs, 'Une barque sur l'océan' (A Boat on the Ocean). Petzold says the idea first came to him while shooting Afire. Laura (Paula Beer), a piano student, survives a serious car accident and is taken in by a grieving family; between her and the lady of the house, Betty (Barbara Auer), a mirror-like resonance slowly develops.
